# Complex analysis {#sec-complex-analysis}

Complex analysis is the calculus of functions of a complex variable that are differentiable in the complex sense.
Such functions are far more rigid than differentiable functions of two real variables: once they are
differentiable they are infinitely differentiable, equal to their Taylor series, determined on a whole domain by
their values on any small piece of it, and their integrals around closed curves are computed by adding up a few
numbers, the residues, attached to the points where the function fails to be defined. This chapter develops that
rigidity in five sections. Complex numbers and functions sets up the field $\mathbb{C}$, modulus and argument, the
exponential and the many-valued logarithm with its branches and branch cuts. Holomorphic functions defines the
complex derivative, derives the Cauchy-Riemann equations and their consequences for harmonic functions and
angle-preserving maps. Contour integration defines integrals along curves and proves the two theorems of Cauchy
that drive everything else, with Liouville's theorem as a first consequence. Series and residues treats Taylor and
Laurent expansions, classifies isolated singularities and states the residue theorem, the tool that evaluates
the real integrals of physics (Fourier transforms, propagators, dispersion relations) in a few lines. Analytic
continuation and special functions extends functions beyond their original domain of definition, introduces the
Gamma, Beta and zeta functions that appear in every dimensional regularisation and every loop integral, and
explains Wick rotation as a deformation of a contour of integration. Each definition is followed by three examples
of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions; each section closes with a
proposition that collects its explicit computations, and the quoted theorems
(Cauchy, Liouville, the residue theorem) are stated with their hypotheses and argued in the text. The reader who
knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the conventions for the signature and for
indices are fixed in @sec-conventions, and the real analysis assumed here (limits, series, the Riemann integral,
partial derivatives) is that of @sec-sequences-limits, @sec-series, @sec-riemann-integral and @sec-calculus.

## Complex numbers and functions {#sec-complex-numbers}

The field $\mathbb{C}$, modulus and argument, the exponential and the logarithm, branches and branch cuts. The six
notions of this section are the vocabulary of the chapter; the single proposition at its end, on the roots of
unity, exercises all of them on explicit numbers.

and the six sixth roots of unity on the unit circle. Right: the imaginary part of the principal logarithm,

### Complex numbers

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-complex-number}
#### Complex number

A **complex number** is a pair of real numbers written $z = x + iy$, with $x = \operatorname{Re} z$ the **real
part**, $y = \operatorname{Im} z$ the **imaginary part** and $i$ a symbol with $i^2 = -1$. Complex numbers are added
componentwise and multiplied by expanding and using $i^2 = -1$: $(x + iy)(u + iv) = (xu - yv) + i(xv + yu)$. With
these operations the set $\mathbb{C}$ of complex numbers is a field: every $z \neq 0$ has an inverse. The
**complex conjugate** of $z$ is $\bar z = x - iy$; conjugation respects sums and products, $\overline{z + w} = \bar
z + \bar w$ and $\overline{zw} = \bar z \bar w$. As a real vector space (@sec-vector-spaces) $\mathbb{C}$ is
$\mathbb{R}^2$ with basis $1, i$, and $z$ is the point $(x, y)$ of the **complex plane** (@fig-complex-plane).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The definition is best absorbed by computing. The first example multiplies and divides two concrete numbers, and shows the one trick that division needs: clearing the denominator with its conjugate.

::: {#exm-complex-arithmetic-basic}
#### A product and a quotient

$(2 + i)(3 - i) = 6 - 2i + 3i - i^2 = 7 + i$, and $\dfrac{1}{2 + i} = \dfrac{2 - i}{(2 + i)(2 - i)} = \dfrac{2 -
i}{5}$: to divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which makes the
denominator real.
:::

The next example looks at what the new symbol $i$ buys. Negative numbers acquire square roots, and polynomials that were irreducible over the reals split into linear factors.

::: {#exm-complex-square-roots}
#### Square roots of negative numbers

$(\pm 2i)^2 = -4$, so $-4$ has the two square roots $\pm 2i$; more generally every non-zero complex number has
exactly two square roots, $w$ and $-w$ (@def-branch below says which one deserves the name $\sqrt z$).
$x^2 + 1 = (x + i)(x - i)$ factorises over $\mathbb{C}$ though not over $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

The third example gives complex multiplication a geometric meaning that the chapter will use repeatedly. A complex number acts on the plane as a matrix of a very special shape, a rotation combined with a scaling.

::: {#exm-complex-matrices}
#### Complex numbers as $2 \times 2$ real matrices

The map $x + iy \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} x & -y \\ y & x \end{pmatrix}$ turns sums into sums and products into matrix
products ($i$ becomes the rotation by $90^\circ$, whose square is $-1$); the determinant of the matrix is $x^2 +
y^2 = |z|^2$ and its transpose represents $\bar z$. Multiplication by a fixed $z$ is thus a rotation-scaling of the
plane, the geometric fact behind @def-conformal.
:::

The first exercise is pure practice with the arithmetic rules. It also introduces Sage's exact Gaussian rationals, which will serve as the computational ground for most of the chapter.

::: {#exr-complex-arithmetic}
#### Products, quotients and conjugates

Compute $(2 + i)(3 - i)$, $(1 + i)/(1 - i)$ and $(1 + i)^8$, and check on these numbers that $\overline{zw} = \bar
z \bar w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(2 + i)(3 - i) = 7 + i$; $(1 + i)/(1 - i) = (1 + i)^2/2 = i$; $(1 + i)^2 = 2i$, so $(1 + i)^8 = (2i)^4 = 16$.

The second exercise derives the small identities that convert between the Cartesian description $(x, y)$ and the pair $(z, \bar z)$. They are used silently in every later computation with real and imaginary parts.

::: {#exr-complex-conjugate-identities}
#### Real and imaginary parts from the conjugate

Show that $\operatorname{Re} z = \tfrac12(z + \bar z)$, $\operatorname{Im} z = \tfrac1{2i}(z - \bar z)$, $z \bar z
= x^2 + y^2$, and that $z$ is real exactly when $z = \bar z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $z = x + iy$: $z + \bar z = 2x$, $z - \bar z = 2iy$, and $z\bar z = (x + iy)(x - iy) = x^2 - i^2 y^2 = x^2 +
y^2$. $z = \bar z$ means $2iy = 0$, that is, $y = 0$. These identities let one translate any statement about
$(x, y)$ into one about $(z, \bar z)$, which is how the Cauchy-Riemann equations are written as $\partial f/\partial
\bar z = 0$ in @exr-cr-polar.
:::

The last exercise on this definition is structural rather than computational. It confirms that $\mathbb{C}$ is a field and explains why inequalities between complex numbers never appear in this chapter.

::: {#exr-complex-field-axioms}
#### The inverse and the impossibility of an order

Show that every $z \neq 0$ has an inverse, $z^{-1} = \bar z/(z \bar z)$, and that $\mathbb{C}$ cannot be given an
order $<$ compatible with its arithmetic in the way $\mathbb{R}$ is (positive numbers closed under sums and products,
every number positive, zero or negative).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$z \cdot \bar z/(z \bar z) = 1$, and $z\bar z = x^2 + y^2 > 0$ when $z \neq 0$. In an ordered field every non-zero
square is positive; $i^2 = -1$ and $1^2 = 1$ would both be positive, so $-1$ and $1$ would be, and their sum $0$
would be positive, a contradiction. Inequalities in this chapter therefore always concern real quantities such as
the modulus.
:::

### Modulus

Having the arithmetic, we need a notion of size. The modulus measures the distance of a point from the origin and turns the complex plane into the metric space on which limits, continuity and open sets make sense.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-modulus}
#### Modulus

The **modulus** (or absolute value) of $z = x + iy$ is $|z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{z \bar z}$, the Euclidean
length of the vector $(x, y)$. It is multiplicative, $|zw| = |z||w|$, and satisfies the **triangle inequality**
$|z + w| \leq |z| + |w|$; $|z - w|$ is the distance between the points $z$ and $w$, so $\mathbb{C}$ is a metric
space with the open discs $D(z_0, r) = \{z : |z - z_0| < r\}$ as basic open sets (the topology of
@sec-topology). A set is **open**, **closed**, **compact** or **connected** in $\mathbb{C}$ exactly when it is so
in $\mathbb{R}^2$; a **domain** is a non-empty open connected set.
:::

The second example singles out the set where the modulus equals one. It is at the same time a curve, a group under multiplication and the contour over which most of the chapter's integrals will be taken.

::: {#exm-modulus-circle}
#### The unit circle

$\{z : |z| = 1\}$ is the unit circle; it is closed under multiplication and inversion ($|zw| = |z||w|$, $|1/z| =
1/|z|$) and so is a group, the group $U(1)$ of phases. $\{|z| < 1\}$ is the open unit disc, a domain; $\{|z| \leq
1\}$ is compact.
:::

The third example turns the triangle inequality around to bound a modulus from below. Lower bounds on denominators are what make large contours negligible later, so this small estimate deserves attention.

::: {#exm-modulus-reverse-triangle}
#### The reverse triangle inequality

From $|z| = |(z - w) + w| \leq |z - w| + |w|$ and the same with $z, w$ exchanged, $\bigl||z| - |w|\bigr| \leq |z -
w|$. It gives lower bounds for denominators: on the circle $|z| = 2$, $|z^2 + 1| \geq |z|^2 - 1 = 3$, the kind of
estimate that makes large arcs of contours negligible in @sec-residues.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves the triangle inequality from the algebra of conjugates. The proof is two lines, but the case of equality is worth understanding geometrically.

::: {#exr-modulus-triangle}
#### The triangle inequality

Prove $|z + w| \leq |z| + |w|$ from $|z + w|^2 = (z + w)(\bar z + \bar w)$ and $\operatorname{Re}(z \bar w) \leq |
z||w|$, and determine when equality holds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|z + w|^2 = |z|^2 + |w|^2 + z\bar w + \bar z w = |z|^2 + |w|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(z\bar w) \leq |z|^2 + |w|^2 +
2|z||w| = (|z| + |w|)^2$, using $\operatorname{Re} u \leq |u|$ and $|z \bar w| = |z||w|$. Equality needs
$\operatorname{Re}(z\bar w) = |z\bar w|$, that is, $z\bar w \geq 0$: $z$ and $w$ point in the same direction (one is
a non-negative multiple of the other).
:::

The second exercise turns a condition on distances into a familiar curve. It is a first instance of translating a statement about moduli into a statement about coordinates.

::: {#exr-modulus-circle-equation}
#### A circle given by a ratio of distances

Show that the set $\{z : |z - 1| = 2|z + 1|\}$ is a circle, and find its centre and radius.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Squaring, $(x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 4\bigl((x + 1)^2 + y^2\bigr)$, that is, $3x^2 + 3y^2 + 10x + 3 = 0$, or $(x +
\tfrac53)^2 + y^2 = \tfrac{16}9$: the circle of centre $-\tfrac53$ and radius $\tfrac43$ (an Apollonius circle).
Sage completes the square:

{{< sage exr-modulus-circle-equation >}}
:::

The third exercise connects the modulus to the Euclidean inner product of @sec-bilinear-forms. The parallelogram law is the identity that characterises norms coming from inner products.

::: {#exr-modulus-parallelogram}
#### The parallelogram law

Prove $|z + w|^2 + |z - w|^2 = 2|z|^2 + 2|w|^2$ and interpret it geometrically; then show that a modulus coming
from an inner product must satisfy it, so that the modulus is the norm of the Euclidean inner product
$\langle z, w \rangle = \operatorname{Re}(z \bar w)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding as in @exr-modulus-triangle, the cross terms $\pm 2\operatorname{Re}(z\bar w)$ cancel between $|z +
w|^2$ and $|z - w|^2$, leaving $2|z|^2 + 2|w|^2$: the sum of the squares of the diagonals of a parallelogram is
the sum of the squares of its four sides. $\operatorname{Re}(z\bar w) = xu + yv$ is the dot product of $(x, y)$
and $(u, v)$ (the Euclidean bilinear form of @sec-bilinear-forms), and $\langle z, z \rangle = |z|^2$.
:::

### Argument

The modulus is only half of the polar description of a complex number. The other half is the angle, and the subtlety that it is defined only up to multiples of $2\pi$ is the seed of every branch cut in this chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-argument}
#### Argument

An **argument** of $z \neq 0$ is any real $\theta$ with $z = |z|(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$; the arguments of $z$
form the set $\arg z = \{\theta_0 + 2\pi k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, and the one in $(-\pi, \pi]$ is the **principal
argument** $\operatorname{Arg} z$. The expression $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ with $r = |z|$ is the **polar
form**; multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments, $\arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w$ as sets modulo
$2\pi$, which for the principal value holds only up to a multiple of $2\pi$. The argument of $0$ is undefined.
:::

The first example lists principal arguments of the simplest numbers and locates the discontinuity. Keep the picture of the negative real axis as the line across which the principal argument jumps.

::: {#exm-argument-values}
#### Principal arguments

$\operatorname{Arg} 1 = 0$, $\operatorname{Arg} i = \pi/2$, $\operatorname{Arg}(-1) = \pi$, $\operatorname{Arg}(-i)
= -\pi/2$, $\operatorname{Arg}(2 + i) = \arctan\tfrac12 \approx 0.4636$ (@fig-complex-plane). A number just below
the negative real axis has principal argument near $-\pi$, one just above near $+\pi$: $\operatorname{Arg}$ is
discontinuous across the negative real axis.
:::

The second example exploits the additivity of arguments to derive trigonometric identities at no cost. Powers of a number on the unit circle multiply its angle, which is de Moivre's formula.

::: {#exm-argument-de-moivre}
#### De Moivre's formula

Multiplying polar forms $n$ times, $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta$. Expanding the
left side for $n = 3$ and comparing real and imaginary parts gives $\cos 3\theta = \cos^3\theta -
3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin 3\theta = 3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta - \sin^3\theta$, the case $n = 3$ recorded
in @prp-roots-of-unity.
:::

The third example is a warning. Additivity holds for the set of all arguments, but the single-valued principal argument can be off by $2\pi$, a discrepancy that will recur for the logarithm.

::: {#exm-argument-product-failure}
#### Where the principal argument fails to add

$\operatorname{Arg}(-1) + \operatorname{Arg}(-1) = 2\pi$, but $\operatorname{Arg}\bigl((-1)(-1)\bigr) =
\operatorname{Arg} 1 = 0$. The set-valued statement $\arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w$ is true ($2\pi \equiv 0$); the
single-valued one is off by $2\pi$. The same failure reappears for the logarithm in @exm-log-product.
:::

The first exercise is a drill in reading off moduli and principal arguments by quadrant. The last item uses de Moivre's formula to avoid expanding a tenth power.

::: {#exr-argument-values}
#### Computing arguments

Find the modulus and principal argument of $-1 - i$, $1 - i\sqrt3$, $-2i$ and $(1 + i)^{10}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|-1 - i| = \sqrt2$ with $\operatorname{Arg} = -3\pi/4$ (third quadrant); $|1 - i\sqrt3| = 2$ with $\operatorname{Arg}
= -\pi/3$; $|-2i| = 2$ with $\operatorname{Arg} = -\pi/2$; $1 + i = \sqrt2\, e^{i\pi/4}$, so $(1 + i)^{10} = 2^5
e^{10 i\pi/4} = 32 e^{i\pi/2} = 32 i$, modulus $32$ and argument $\pi/2$:

{{< sage exr-argument-values >}}
:::

The second exercise proves the addition rule for arguments from the addition formulas of trigonometry. It then asks for an explicit failure of the rule for principal values.

::: {#exr-argument-multiplicative}
#### Arguments of products and quotients

Prove $\arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w$ and $\arg(1/z) = -\arg z$ as sets modulo $2\pi$ from the addition formulas for
sine and cosine, and give an example in which $\operatorname{Arg}(z/w) \neq \operatorname{Arg} z -
\operatorname{Arg} w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\, s(\cos\phi + i\sin\phi) = rs\bigl[(\cos\theta\cos\phi - \sin\theta\sin\phi) +
i(\sin\theta\cos\phi + \cos\theta\sin\phi)\bigr] = rs\bigl(\cos(\theta + \phi) + i\sin(\theta + \phi)\bigr)$, so
$\theta + \phi$ is an argument of $zw$; every argument of $zw$ differs from it by a multiple of $2\pi$. For $1/z$,
$1/z = \bar z/|z|^2 = r^{-1}(\cos\theta - i\sin\theta) = r^{-1}(\cos(-\theta) + i\sin(-\theta))$. Example: $z = -
1$, $w = i$: $\operatorname{Arg}(z/w) = \operatorname{Arg}(i) = \pi/2$, while $\operatorname{Arg} z -
\operatorname{Arg} w = \pi - \pi/2 = \pi/2$; take instead $z = -1$, $w = -i$: $z/w = -i$ has $\operatorname{Arg} =
-\pi/2$ but $\pi - (-\pi/2) = 3\pi/2$.
:::

The third exercise solves a polynomial equation by polar form alone. The same method gives all $n$-th roots of any complex number, and the roots always form a regular polygon
centred at the origin.

::: {#exr-argument-roots-polynomial}
#### Solving $z^4 = -16$

Write $-16$ in polar form and find all four solutions of $z^4 = -16$ in polar and in Cartesian form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-16 = 16 e^{i\pi}$, so $z = 2 e^{i(\pi + 2\pi k)/4}$, $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$: the arguments $\pi/4, 3\pi/4, 5\pi/4,
7\pi/4$ give $z = \sqrt2(\pm 1 \pm i)$. The four roots lie on the circle of radius $2$ at the corners of a square;
Sage finds them as algebraic numbers:

{{< sage exr-argument-roots-polynomial >}}
:::

### The complex exponential

The exponential is the most important function of the chapter. Defined by its power series, it ties the polar form to the arithmetic of $\mathbb{C}$ through Euler's formula and makes trigonometry a chapter of complex analysis.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-complex-exponential}
#### Complex exponential

The **complex exponential** is $e^z = \exp z = \sum_{n \geq 0} z^n/n!$, a series that converges absolutely for
every $z$ (compare the ratio test of @sec-series); equivalently, by multiplying the series, $e^{x + iy} = e^x(\cos
y + i\sin y)$ (**Euler's formula**). It satisfies $e^{z + w} = e^z e^w$, never vanishes, has $|e^{x + iy}| = e^x$
and $\arg e^{x + iy} \ni y$, and is periodic with period $2\pi i$. The polar form becomes $z = r e^{i\theta}$. The
trigonometric and hyperbolic functions are defined from it: $\cos z = \tfrac12(e^{iz} + e^{-iz})$, $\sin z =
\tfrac1{2i}(e^{iz} - e^{-iz})$, $\cosh z = \tfrac12(e^z + e^{-z})$, $\sinh z = \tfrac12(e^z - e^{-z})$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example evaluates the exponential on the imaginary axis. The values show that the exponential wraps a line around a circle, which is the origin of its periodicity.

::: {#exm-exp-euler-identity}
#### Euler's identity

$e^{i\pi} = \cos\pi + i\sin\pi = -1$, $e^{i\pi/2} = i$, $e^{2\pi i} = 1$: the exponential wraps the imaginary axis
around the unit circle, and $e^{z + 2\pi i} = e^z$ for every $z$.
:::

The second example uses the exponential to write down all solutions of $z^n = 1$ at once. The picture is a regular polygon on the unit circle, drawn for $n = 6$ in @fig-complex-plane.

::: {#exm-exp-roots-of-unity}
#### Roots of unity as exponentials

The solutions of $z^n = 1$ are $\omega_k = e^{2\pi i k/n}$, $k = 0, \dots, n - 1$, the $n$-th **roots of unity**;
they form a regular $n$-gon on the unit circle (@fig-complex-plane shows $n = 6$), and $\omega_1^k = \omega_k$,
so they are the powers of a single one (@prp-roots-of-unity).
:::

The third example evaluates cosine and sine at imaginary arguments. The result is that bounded real functions become unbounded in the plane, a fact Liouville's theorem will later explain.

::: {#exm-exp-trig-complex}
#### Trigonometric functions of a complex argument

$\cos(iy) = \tfrac12(e^{-y} + e^{y}) = \cosh y$ and $\sin(iy) = i\sinh y$: on the imaginary axis the cosine grows
without bound. $|\cos z|$ is therefore not bounded by $1$ on $\mathbb{C}$, which is why a bounded function like
$\cos x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has no bounded extension to the plane (@cor-liouville).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes a few values of the exponential in Cartesian form. It is a test of Euler's formula and of the periodicity in the imaginary direction.

::: {#exr-exp-values}
#### Values of the exponential

Compute $e^{1 + i\pi}$, $e^{i\pi/2}$, $e^{\ln 2 + i\pi/3}$ and $e^{3\pi i/2}$ in Cartesian form, and verify
$e^{z + 2\pi i} = e^z$ for $z = 1 + i$ numerically.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{1 + i\pi} = -e$; $e^{i\pi/2} = i$; $e^{\ln 2 + i\pi/3} = 2(\tfrac12 + i\tfrac{\sqrt3}2) = 1 + i\sqrt3$;
$e^{3\pi i/2} = -i$:

{{< sage exr-exp-values >}}

The second exercise derives the addition formulas of trigonometry from the exponential. Nothing about the argument requires $z$ and $w$ to be real, which is the point.

::: {#exr-exp-trig}
#### Addition formulas from the exponential

Derive $\cos(z + w) = \cos z\cos w - \sin z\sin w$ and $\cos^2 z + \sin^2 z = 1$ for complex $z, w$ from the
definitions in @def-complex-exponential and $e^{z + w} = e^z e^w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\cos z\cos w - \sin z\sin w = \tfrac14(e^{iz} + e^{-iz})(e^{iw} + e^{-iw}) + \tfrac14(e^{iz} - e^{-iz})(e^{iw} -
e^{-iw}) = \tfrac12(e^{i(z + w)} + e^{-i(z + w)}) = \cos(z + w)$. Setting $w = -z$ and using $\cos(-z) = \cos z$,
$\sin(-z) = -\sin z$ gives $\cos^2 z + \sin^2 z = \cos 0 = 1$. The identities proved for real arguments in
trigonometry thus hold verbatim for complex ones, a first instance of the identity theorem of
@def-analytic-continuation.
:::

The third exercise determines the image of the exponential and the preimages of a given value. Its answer explains why the inverse function, the logarithm, must be many-valued.

::: {#exr-exp-surjective}
#### The image of the exponential

Show that $e^z \neq 0$ for every $z$, that every $w \neq 0$ equals $e^z$ for some $z$, and find all solutions of
$e^z = -1$ and of $e^z = 1 + i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^z e^{-z} = e^0 = 1$, so $e^z$ has an inverse and is non-zero. Given $w = |w| e^{i\theta} \neq 0$, $z = \ln|w| +
i\theta$ satisfies $e^z = w$, and so does $z + 2\pi i k$. $e^z = -1 = e^{i\pi}$ gives $z = i\pi + 2\pi i k$; $e^z
= 1 + i = \sqrt2 e^{i\pi/4}$ gives $z = \tfrac12\ln 2 + i(\pi/4 + 2\pi k)$. The exponential is onto
$\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ and infinitely-many-to-one, which is why its inverse, the logarithm, is many-valued.
:::

### The complex logarithm

Inverting the exponential is the first place where many-valuedness becomes unavoidable. The logarithm is defined as a set of values, and a principal choice is made so that formulas have a definite meaning.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-complex-logarithm}
#### Complex logarithm

A **logarithm** of $z \neq 0$ is any $w$ with $e^w = z$; the logarithms of $z$ form the set $\log z = \ln|z| +
i\arg z = \{\ln|z| + i(\operatorname{Arg} z + 2\pi k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. The **principal logarithm** is
$\operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + i\operatorname{Arg} z$, with imaginary part in $(-\pi, \pi]$. Complex powers are
defined through the logarithm, $z^a = e^{a\log z}$ (many-valued in general), with the **principal power** $e^{a
\operatorname{Log} z}$; for integer $a$ all values agree, for $a = 1/n$ there are $n$ values, the $n$-th roots.
:::

The second example revisits the failure of additivity seen for the argument. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms only as sets, not for the principal values.

::: {#exm-log-product}
#### The logarithm of a product

$\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1) = 2\pi i$, but $\operatorname{Log}\bigl((-1)(-1)\bigr) = 0$
(@prp-roots-of-unity records the check). The set identity $\log(zw) = \log z + \log w$ holds; the principal
values satisfy it only up to $2\pi i k$. Any formula manipulation with complex logarithms must track which branch
is meant.
:::

The third example computes a complex power of a complex number. The surprise is that $i^i$ is real, and that it is not one number but infinitely many.

::: {#exm-log-i-to-the-i}
#### $i^i$

$i^i = e^{i\log i} = e^{i(i\pi/2 + 2\pi i k)} = e^{-\pi/2 - 2\pi k}$: all values are real, the principal one being
$e^{-\pi/2} \approx 0.2079$. A complex power of a complex number is a set of numbers, and which member is meant is
a matter of convention (the principal one unless stated otherwise).
:::

The second exercise characterises exactly when the principal logarithm is additive. The answer identifies the right half-plane as a region where no bookkeeping of branches is needed.

::: {#exr-log-product-failure}
#### When does $\operatorname{Log}(zw) = \operatorname{Log} z + \operatorname{Log} w$?

Show that the principal logarithm is additive exactly when $\operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w \in (-\pi,
\pi]$, and deduce that it is additive whenever $\operatorname{Re} z > 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} w > 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\ln|zw| = \ln|z| + \ln|w|$ always, and $\operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w$ is an argument of $zw$; it
is the principal one exactly when it lies in $(-\pi, \pi]$. If both real parts are positive, both principal
arguments lie in $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ and their sum in $(-\pi, \pi)$. Hence $\operatorname{Log}$ is additive on the
right half-plane, where it is also continuous and, as @sec-holomorphic shows, holomorphic.
:::

#### The two square roots as two branches

Show that $z^{1/2} = e^{\frac12\log z}$ takes exactly two values, $\pm\sqrt{|z|}\, e^{i\operatorname{Arg}(z)/2}$,
and that the principal one maps $\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty, 0]$ onto the right half-plane; compute the principal

z \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, so it lies in the right half-plane (or on the positive imaginary axis for negative $z$).
The two nearby points have principal roots near $+i$ and $-i$ respectively: the principal square root jumps by a
sign across its branch cut:

### Branches

The repeated appearance of a choice among many values deserves a name. A branch is a continuous selection of one value, and a branch cut is the price paid for it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-branch}
#### Branch

Let $F$ be a many-valued function such as $\log$ or $z^{1/n}$. A **branch** of $F$ on a domain $D$ is a
continuous function $f : D \to \mathbb{C}$ with $f(z) \in F(z)$ for every $z \in D$. A **branch point** is a point
around which no branch exists on any punctured neighbourhood (circling it once changes the value), and a
**branch cut** is a curve removed from the plane so that a branch exists on the remainder; the principal branch
of $\log$ and of $z^a$ uses the cut $(-\infty, 0]$, with branch point $0$. The branch of $\sqrt z$ on
$\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty, 0]$ with $\sqrt 1 = 1$ is the principal square root.
:::

The first example lists the branches of the logarithm on the slit plane and explains why none exists on the punctured plane. A loop around the origin changes the value, so the origin is a branch point.

::: {#exm-branch-log}
#### Branches of the logarithm

On $\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty, 0]$ every function $\operatorname{Log} z + 2\pi i k$ is a branch of $\log$;
there is no branch on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, since following $\ln|z| + i\theta$ once around the unit circle
increases it by $2\pi i$ (the origin is a branch point). A different cut, such as $[0, +\infty)$ with $\arg z
\in (0, 2\pi)$, gives another family of branches, continuous across the negative axis and discontinuous across the
positive one.
:::

The second example does the same for the square root, where a loop changes the sign. Two loops restore the value, which is the first glimpse of a two-sheeted Riemann surface.

::: {#exm-branch-sqrt}
#### The square root and its sign flip

Going once around $0$ along $z = e^{i\theta}$, the continuous choice $\sqrt z = e^{i\theta/2}$ returns to
$e^{i\pi} = -1$ instead of $1$: $0$ is a branch point of $\sqrt z$. Two circuits restore the value, which is
why the two branches of the square root are swapped by a loop and why the natural domain of $\sqrt z$ is a
two-sheeted surface glued along the cut (a Riemann surface).
:::

The third example has two branch points and shows that the cut may join them or run from each to infinity. Both choices give a branch, and the application decides between them.

::: {#exm-branch-sqrt-z2-minus-1}
#### A function with two branch points

$\sqrt{z^2 - 1} = \sqrt{z - 1}\sqrt{z + 1}$ has branch points $\pm 1$. Circling both at once multiplies the value by
$(-1)(-1) = 1$, so a branch exists on $\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1, 1]$ (the cut joins the branch points) as well as on
$\mathbb{C}\setminus\bigl((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\bigr)$; which cut is used depends on where one needs the
function continuous (@exr-branch-sqrt-z2-1).
:::

The first exercise measures the jumps of the principal square root and logarithm numerically. It also confirms that there is no jump across the positive real axis.

::: {#exr-branch-sqrt-continuity}
#### The jump across the cut

Evaluate the principal $\sqrt{z}$ and the principal $\operatorname{Log} z$ at $z = -4 \pm 10^{-6} i$ and show
numerically that the square root jumps by $4i$ and the logarithm by $2\pi i$ across the negative real axis, while
both are continuous across the positive one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Above the cut $\operatorname{Arg} \approx \pi$, below $\approx -\pi$, so $\sqrt{-4 \pm i\epsilon} \to \pm 2i$ and
$\operatorname{Log}(-4 \pm i\epsilon) \to \ln 4 \pm i\pi$; at $+4 \pm i\epsilon$ both functions return $2$ and
$\ln 4$ up to $O(\epsilon)$:

{{< sage exr-branch-sqrt-continuity >}}
:::

The second exercise constructs a branch of the logarithm with a different cut. Comparing it with the principal branch shows where two branches agree and where they differ by $2\pi i$.

::: {#exr-branch-cut-choice}
#### A branch of the logarithm on the slit plane

Define a branch of $\log$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus[0, +\infty)$ with $\log(-1) = i\pi$, give its values at $i$ and
$-i$, and compare them with the principal values.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $\arg z \in (0, 2\pi)$ and set $\log z = \ln|z| + i\arg z$; it is continuous off the positive real axis and
has $\log(-1) = i\pi$. Then $\log i = i\pi/2$ (same as the principal value) and $\log(-i) = 3\pi i/2$, whereas
$\operatorname{Log}(-i) = -i\pi/2$: the two branches agree in the upper half-plane and differ by $2\pi i$ in the
lower one.
:::

The third exercise builds a branch of $\sqrt{z^2 - 1}$ that looks like $z$ at infinity. Such branches are the ones used in dispersion relations, where the discontinuity across the cut carries the physics.

::: {#exr-branch-sqrt-z2-1}
#### A branch of $\sqrt{z^2 - 1}$ behaving like $z$ at infinity

Show that $f(z) = z\sqrt{1 - 1/z^2}$, with the principal square root, is a branch of $\sqrt{z^2 - 1}$ on
$\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1, 1]$, that $f(z) = z + O(1/z)$ as $|z| \to \infty$, and compute its values just above and
just below the cut at $z = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1 - 1/z^2$ lies on $(-\infty, 0]$ exactly when $1/z^2 \geq 1$, that is, $z \in [-1, 1]$; off that segment the
principal root is continuous, and $f(z)^2 = z^2 - 1$. For large $|z|$, $\sqrt{1 - 1/z^2} = 1 - \tfrac1{2z^2} +
\dots$, so $f(z) = z - \tfrac1{2z} + \dots$. At $z = \pm i\epsilon$, $1 - 1/z^2 = 1 + 1/\epsilon^2 > 0$, so $f(\pm
i\epsilon) = \pm i\epsilon\sqrt{1 + 1/\epsilon^2} \to \pm i$: the branch jumps from $i$ to $-i$ across the cut
at $0$, by the amount $2i$ that makes the discontinuity integrals of @sec-residues work.
:::

### Worked computations

The section closes with explicit facts about roots of unity, moduli and logarithms. Each item is a small computation, and together they exercise every definition of the section.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-roots-of-unity}
#### Sixth roots of unity

The six numbers $\omega_k = e^{2\pi i k/6}$, $k = 0, \dots, 5$, satisfy $\omega_k^6 = 1$; their sum is $0$ and
their product is $-1$; they are the six roots of $z^6 - 1$ in $\mathbb{C}$, and exactly two of them, $\pm1$, are
real. De Moivre's formula holds for $n = 3$, $|2 + i| = \sqrt 5$ with $|z|^2 = z\bar z$, and
$\operatorname{Log}(-1) = i\pi$ with $\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1) \neq
\operatorname{Log}\bigl((-1)^2\bigr)$.
:::

The first example explains the vanishing sum by a geometric series. The argument is the same for any $n$, and it is the finite analogue of Fourier orthogonality.

::: {#exm-roots-sum-geometric}
#### Why the sum vanishes

With $\omega = e^{2\pi i/6}$, the roots are $1, \omega, \dots, \omega^5$, and $(1 + \omega + \dots + \omega^5)(1 -
\omega) = 1 - \omega^6 = 0$ with $\omega \neq 1$, so the sum is zero. The argument works for every $n \geq 2$
(@exr-roots-general).
:::

The second example explains the product in two ways, through the constant term of the polynomial and through the exponent sum. Both are instances of Vieta's relations.

::: {#exm-roots-product}
#### Why the product is $-1$

The product of the roots of the monic polynomial $z^6 - 1$ is $(-1)^6 \cdot (-1) = -1$ (the constant term, up to
sign); directly, $\prod_k \omega^k = \omega^{0 + 1 + \dots + 5} = \omega^{15} = \omega^3 = e^{i\pi} = -1$.
:::

The third example factorises $z^6 - 1$ over the rationals and over the complex numbers. The number of factors depends on the field, a theme taken up in @exr-roots-polynomial-factor.

::: {#exm-roots-factorisation}
#### The factorisation of $z^6 - 1$

Over $\mathbb{Q}$, $z^6 - 1 = (z - 1)(z + 1)(z^2 + z + 1)(z^2 - z + 1)$; the quadratic factors have the four
non-real roots $\omega^{\pm 2}$ and $\omega^{\pm 1}$. Over $\mathbb{C}$ every factor splits into linear ones,
$z^6 - 1 = \prod_k (z - \omega_k)$, as the fundamental theorem of algebra (@exr-liouville-fta) guarantees for
any polynomial.
:::

#### Cube roots of unity

\tfrac12 = 0$, and $\omega^2 = \bar\omega$ because $|\omega| = 1$ gives $\bar\omega = 1/\omega = \omega^{3 - 1}$:

The second exercise generalises the vanishing sum to arbitrary powers of the roots. The result is the discrete orthogonality relation behind the discrete Fourier transform.

::: {#exr-roots-general}
#### Sums of powers of the roots

Prove that for $n \geq 2$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$, $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega^{km}$ equals $n$ if $n$ divides
$m$ and $0$ otherwise.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $n \mid m$ then $\omega^m = 1$ and every term is $1$. Otherwise $\omega^m \neq 1$ and the geometric sum is
$(1 - \omega^{mn})/(1 - \omega^m) = 0$ since $\omega^{mn} = (\omega^n)^m = 1$. This orthogonality of the discrete
exponentials is the finite version of $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(m - n)\theta}\,d\theta = 2\pi\delta_{mn}$ in
@exr-circle-fourier.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

## Holomorphic functions {#sec-holomorphic}

The complex derivative, the Cauchy-Riemann equations, harmonic functions and conformal maps. A function of a
complex variable is differentiable when its difference quotient has a limit that does not depend on the direction
of approach; this single requirement, written out in real and imaginary parts, is the pair of Cauchy-Riemann
equations, and it forces the real and imaginary parts to be harmonic and the map to preserve angles.

![Holomorphic functions seen in two ways. Left: domain colouring of $f(z) = (z - 1)/(z^2 + 1)$, hue encoding
$\arg f(z)$ and brightness $|f(z)|$; the zero at $z = 1$ and the poles at $z = \pm i$ are the points where all hues
meet. Right: the image of the Cartesian grid under $z \mapsto z^2$; the image curves still meet at right angles,
since the map is conformal away from $z = 0$. Generated by
`figures/domain_colouring.sage`.](figures/domain_colouring.svg){#fig-domain-colouring width=95%}

{{< interactive domain_colouring 480 >}}

### The complex derivative

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-complex-derivative}
#### Complex derivative

A function $f : D \to \mathbb{C}$ on an open set $D$ is **complex differentiable** at $z_0 \in D$ if the limit
$$f'(z_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)}{h}, \qquad h \in \mathbb{C},$$
exists; $f'(z_0)$ is the **complex derivative**. The limit is over complex $h$, so the quotient must approach the
same value along every direction. The sum, product, quotient and chain rules hold with the same proofs as in
@sec-continuity-differentiability, and $(z^n)' = n z^{n-1}$, $(e^z)' = e^z$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The first example computes a derivative straight from the limit. The quotient simplifies to an expression without any dependence on the direction of $h$, which is the whole point.

::: {#exm-derivative-z2}
#### $z^2$ from the definition

$\dfrac{(z + h)^2 - z^2}{h} = 2z + h \to 2z$ whatever the direction of $h$: $(z^2)' = 2z$. Likewise $(z^n)' = n
z^{n-1}$ by the binomial theorem.
:::

The second example is the simplest function for which the limit fails. Conjugation is smooth as a map of the plane, so the failure shows how much stronger complex differentiability is than real differentiability.

::: {#exm-derivative-conjugate}
#### $\bar z$ is not complex differentiable

$\dfrac{\overline{z + h} - \bar z}{h} = \dfrac{\bar h}{h}$ equals $1$ for real $h$ and $-1$ for imaginary $h$; the
limit does not exist at any point. Conjugation is a perfectly smooth map of $\mathbb{R}^2$ (a reflection), so
complex differentiability is strictly stronger than real differentiability.
:::

The third example differentiates the exponential from its series. The derivatives of the trigonometric functions follow by the chain rule, with the same formulas as on the real line.

::: {#exm-derivative-exponential}
#### The exponential

From the series, $e^{z + h} - e^z = e^z(e^h - 1) = e^z(h + h^2/2 + \dots)$, so $(e^{z+h} - e^z)/h \to e^z$:
$(e^z)' = e^z$, and by the chain rule $(\cos z)' = -\sin z$, $(\sin z)' = \cos z$.
:::

The first exercise applies the limit definition to two more functions. Watch how the direction of $h$ drops out of the quotient as soon as $\bar h$ never appears.

::: {#exr-derivative-z3}
#### A derivative from the definition

Compute $(z^3)'$ and $(1/z)'$ ($z \neq 0$) directly from the limit of the difference quotient.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\bigl((z + h)^3 - z^3\bigr)/h = 3z^2 + 3zh + h^2 \to 3z^2$. $\bigl(1/(z + h) - 1/z\bigr)/h = -1/\bigl(z(z +
h)\bigr) \to -1/z^2$. Neither limit depends on the direction of $h$, as the quotients are polynomial or rational
in $h$ without any $\bar h$.
:::

The second exercise examines functions in which $\bar z$ does appear. A function may be differentiable at an isolated point, which is not yet holomorphy.

::: {#exr-derivative-conj-fails}
#### Functions of $z$ and $\bar z$

Show that $f(z) = |z|^2 = z\bar z$ is complex differentiable at $z = 0$ and nowhere else, and that
$\operatorname{Re} z$ is complex differentiable nowhere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\bigl(|z + h|^2 - |z|^2\bigr)/h = \bar z + \bar h + z\bar h/h$. At $z = 0$ this is $\bar h \to 0$, so $f'(0) = 0$.
For $z \neq 0$ the term $z\bar h/h$ takes the values $z$ (real $h$) and $-z$ (imaginary $h$), so the limit
fails. For $\operatorname{Re} z$ the quotient is $\operatorname{Re}(h)/h$, equal to $1$ or $0$ along the two axes.
:::

#### The quotient rule on a rational function

### Holomorphic functions

Differentiability at a single point is of little use. The useful notion is differentiability on an open set, which is what holomorphy means and what the rest of the chapter assumes.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-holomorphic}
#### Holomorphic function

A function is **holomorphic** on an open set $D$ if it is complex differentiable at every point of $D$; it is
holomorphic at a point if it is holomorphic on some neighbourhood of it. A function holomorphic on all of
$\mathbb{C}$ is **entire**. Sums, products and compositions of holomorphic functions are holomorphic, and so are
quotients away from the zeros of the denominator.
:::

The first example lists the entire functions met so far and the domains of rational functions. The picture to keep is a plane with a finite number of punctures.

::: {#exm-holomorphic-polynomials}
#### Polynomials and the exponential

Every polynomial is entire, and so are $e^z$, $\cos z$, $\sin z$, $\cosh z$, $\sinh z$ (compositions of
polynomials with the exponential). A rational function $p/q$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}$ minus the zeros of
$q$: $(z - 1)/(z^2 + 1)$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{i, -i\}$ (@fig-domain-colouring).
:::

The second example is the principal logarithm, holomorphic off its cut with the expected derivative. Holomorphy fails on the cut because continuity already does.

::: {#exm-holomorphic-log}
#### The principal logarithm

$\operatorname{Log} z$ is holomorphic on the slit plane $\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty, 0]$ with $\operatorname{Log}'
z = 1/z$ (differentiate $e^{\operatorname{Log} z} = z$ with the chain rule). It is not even continuous on the cut,
so it is not holomorphic there; every other branch of $\log$ is holomorphic off its own cut with the same
derivative $1/z$.
:::

$\bar z$, $\operatorname{Re} z$, $|z|$ and $|z|^2$ are nowhere holomorphic (@exr-derivative-conj-fails): a

The first exercise proves the sum and product rules from the definition. The product rule requires continuity, which differentiability provides.

::: {#exr-holomorphic-polynomials}
#### Closure under the algebraic operations

Using only the limit definition, show that if $f$ and $g$ are holomorphic on $D$ then so are $f + g$ and $fg$,
with $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The sum rule is immediate from the sum of limits. For the product, $f(z + h)g(z + h) - f(z)g(z) = \bigl(f(z + h) -
f(z)\bigr)g(z + h) + f(z)\bigl(g(z + h) - g(z)\bigr)$; dividing by $h$ and using the continuity of $g$ at $z$
(differentiable implies continuous, since $f(z + h) - f(z) = h \cdot$ quotient $\to 0$) gives $f'g + fg'$.
:::

The second exercise finds domains of holomorphy of a rational and of a trigonometric function. Cancelling common factors matters, since a removable singularity is not a genuine one.

::: {#exr-holomorphic-rational-domain}
#### The domain of holomorphy of a rational function

Find the largest open set on which $f(z) = \dfrac{z^2 + 1}{z^4 - 1}$ is holomorphic, after cancelling common
factors, and the set on which $g(z) = \tan z$ is.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$z^4 - 1 = (z^2 + 1)(z^2 - 1)$, so $f = 1/(z^2 - 1)$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1, -1\}$ (the apparent
singularities at $\pm i$ are removable, @def-isolated-singularity). $\tan z = \sin z/\cos z$ is holomorphic where
$\cos z \neq 0$, that is, away from $z = \pi/2 + k\pi$ ($\cos z = 0$ forces $e^{2iz} = -1$, so $z$ is real):

The third exercise uses the Cauchy-Riemann equations, stated next, to show that holomorphic functions of constant modulus are constant. Read the theorem first and then return to it.

::: {#exr-holomorphic-abs}
#### Holomorphic functions with constant modulus

Show that a holomorphic function on a domain with $|f|$ constant is itself constant. (Use the Cauchy-Riemann
equations of @thm-cauchy-riemann once you have read them.)
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $|f| = 0$ then $f = 0$. Otherwise $u^2 + v^2 = c > 0$; differentiating, $u u_x + v v_x = 0$ and $u u_y + v v_y =
0$. With $u_y = -v_x$ and $v_y = u_x$ the second reads $-u v_x + v u_x = 0$. The two equations form a linear
system in $(u_x, v_x)$ with determinant $u^2 + v^2 = c \neq 0$, so $u_x = v_x = 0$, hence also $u_y = v_y = 0$,
and $f$ is constant on the (connected) domain.
:::

### The Cauchy-Riemann equations

The direction-independence of the complex derivative can be written as a pair of partial differential equations. These are the Cauchy-Riemann equations, the computational criterion for holomorphy.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-cauchy-riemann}
#### Cauchy-Riemann equations

Write $f(x + iy) = u(x, y) + iv(x, y)$ with $u, v$ real. If $f$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$ then the partial
derivatives of $u$ and $v$ exist there and satisfy the **Cauchy-Riemann equations**
$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x},$$
with $f'(z_0) = u_x + iv_x$. Conversely, if $u, v$ are continuously differentiable on an open set and satisfy the
Cauchy-Riemann equations there, then $f$ is holomorphic on it. The equations say that the real Jacobian of $(x, y)
\mapsto (u, v)$ has the form $\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}$, the matrix of multiplication by $a +
ib = f'$ (@exm-complex-matrices).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The third example shows the equations failing for conjugation. The Jacobian is a reflection, whose determinant is negative, and no complex number multiplies like that.

::: {#exm-cr-conjugate}
#### $\bar z$ fails

$\bar z = x - iy$ has $u_x = 1 \neq -1 = v_y$: the first Cauchy-Riemann equation fails everywhere, in agreement with
@exm-derivative-conjugate. The Jacobian $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$ is a reflection, not a rotation-scaling.
:::

The second exercise rewrites the equations with the Wirtinger derivatives. The slogan that a holomorphic function does not depend on $\bar z$ becomes a literal statement.

::: {#exr-cr-polar}
#### The Wirtinger form

Define the operators $\partial_z = \tfrac12(\partial_x - i\partial_y)$ and $\partial_{\bar z} = \tfrac12(\partial_x +
i\partial_y)$. Show that the Cauchy-Riemann equations are equivalent to $\partial_{\bar z} f = 0$, and that
then $f' = \partial_z f$. Check both on $f = z^2$ and on $f = z\bar z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_{\bar z}(u + iv) = \tfrac12\bigl[(u_x - v_y) + i(u_y + v_x)\bigr]$, which vanishes exactly when both
Cauchy-Riemann equations hold; then $\partial_z f = \tfrac12\bigl[(u_x + v_y) + i(v_x - u_y)\bigr] = u_x + iv_x =
f'$. Treating $z$ and $\bar z$ as independent variables, $\partial_{\bar z}(z^2) = 0$ and $\partial_z(z^2) = 2z$,
while $\partial_{\bar z}(z\bar z) = z \neq 0$ except at the origin (@exr-derivative-conj-fails).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `ideal_membership`, certificate `ca-holo-ring.sage`; Test (kernel-checked, 4 instances); script `ca-holo-wirtinger-test.sage`.

The third exercise draws two rigidity consequences from the equations. Real-valued holomorphic functions and holomorphic functions with vanishing derivative are both constant.

::: {#exr-cr-constant}
#### Holomorphic functions with real values

Prove that a holomorphic function on a domain whose values are all real is constant, and that a holomorphic
function whose derivative vanishes identically is constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $v = 0$ then $u_x = v_y = 0$ and $u_y = -v_x = 0$, so $u$ is constant on the connected open set (a function
with vanishing gradient is constant along every path, @sec-calculus). If $f' = u_x + iv_x = 0$ then $u_x = v_x
= 0$ and, by the equations, $u_y = v_y = 0$, so both $u$ and $v$ are constant.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

### Harmonic functions

The Cauchy-Riemann equations have a consequence for each of $u$ and $v$ separately. Both satisfy Laplace's equation, the equation of electrostatics and of steady heat flow in the plane.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-harmonic}
#### Harmonic function

A twice continuously differentiable real function $u$ on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is **harmonic** if it
satisfies Laplace's equation $\Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$. If $f = u + iv$ is holomorphic then $u$ and $v$
are harmonic (differentiate the Cauchy-Riemann equations and use $u_{xy} = u_{yx}$), and $v$ is called a
**harmonic conjugate** of $u$; on a disc every harmonic $u$ has a harmonic conjugate, unique up to an additive
constant.
:::

The first example checks harmonicity on the parts of $z^2$ and gives a non-example. The function $x^2 + y^2$ is smooth and positive but is the real part of nothing holomorphic.

::: {#exm-harmonic-polynomial}
#### $x^2 - y^2$ and $2xy$

$u = x^2 - y^2$ has $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 2 - 2 = 0$, and its harmonic conjugate is $v = 2xy$, the imaginary part of
$z^2$ (@prp-cauchy-riemann-examples). $x^2 + y^2$ is not harmonic ($\Delta = 4$): it is the real part of no
holomorphic function.
:::

The second example takes the parts of the exponential. Any entire function supplies harmonic functions on the whole plane in this way.

::: {#exm-harmonic-exp}
#### $e^x\cos y$

$u = e^x\cos y$ has $u_{xx} = e^x\cos y$ and $u_{yy} = -e^x\cos y$, so it is harmonic, with conjugate $e^x\sin y$:
together they are $e^z$. More generally the real part of any entire function is a harmonic function on the whole
plane.
:::

The third example is the logarithmic potential, harmonic on the punctured plane. Its conjugate is the angle, which exists locally but not globally, mirroring the branch point of the logarithm.

::: {#exm-harmonic-log}
#### $\ln|z|$ and the angle

$u = \ln\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ is harmonic on $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$ (it is the real part of any branch of $\log
z$), the two-dimensional Coulomb potential of a point charge. Its conjugate $\arg z$ exists on every disc not
containing $0$ but not on the whole punctured plane: the branch point obstructs a global conjugate, the harmonic
counterpart of @exm-branch-log.
:::

The first exercise constructs a harmonic conjugate by integrating the Cauchy-Riemann equations. The resulting holomorphic function is recognisable at the end.

::: {#exr-harmonic-conjugate}
#### Finding a harmonic conjugate

Show that $u = x^3 - 3xy^2$ is harmonic, find its harmonic conjugate $v$ with $v(0, 0) = 0$ by integrating the
Cauchy-Riemann equations, and identify $u + iv$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u_{xx} = 6x$, $u_{yy} = -6x$. From $v_y = u_x = 3x^2 - 3y^2$, $v = 3x^2 y - y^3 + c(x)$; then $v_x = 6xy + c'(x)$
must equal $-u_y = 6xy$, so $c$ is constant, zero by the normalisation. $u + iv = x^3 - 3xy^2 + i(3x^2 y - y^3) =
(x + iy)^3 = z^3$:

{{< sage exr-harmonic-conjugate >}}
:::

The second exercise derives the mean value property from Cauchy's integral formula, which is stated in the next section. The maximum principle follows in one sentence.

::: {#exr-harmonic-mean-value}
#### The mean value property

Assuming Cauchy's integral formula (@thm-cauchy-integral-formula), show that a harmonic function on a disc equals
at the centre the average of its values on any concentric circle inside the disc, and deduce that it cannot have
a strict local maximum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $f = u + iv$ be holomorphic on the disc with $u$ the given function. With $z = z_0 + re^{i\theta}$, $dz = i
re^{i\theta}d\theta$, the integral formula reads $f(z_0) = \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(z_0 + re^{i\theta})\,
d\theta$; its real part is the mean value property. If $u(z_0)$ were strictly larger than all nearby values, the
average over a small circle would be strictly smaller than $u(z_0)$, contradicting the property.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The third exercise rewrites the Laplacian in polar coordinates with the chain rule of @sec-calculus. The functions $r^n\cos n\theta$ are then seen to be harmonic for every $n$.

::: {#exr-harmonic-polar}
#### Laplace's equation in polar coordinates

Using the chain rule of @sec-calculus, show that in polar coordinates $\Delta u = u_{rr} + \tfrac1r u_r +
\tfrac1{r^2}u_{\theta\theta}$, and verify that $r^n\cos n\theta$ is harmonic for every integer $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$ one has $u_x = \cos\theta\, u_r - \tfrac{\sin\theta}r u_\theta$ and $u_y =
\sin\theta\, u_r + \tfrac{\cos\theta}r u_\theta$; applying the same operators again and adding, the cross terms
cancel and the stated form results. For $u = r^n\cos n\theta$: $u_{rr} + \tfrac1r u_r = n(n - 1)r^{n-2}\cos
n\theta + nr^{n-2}\cos n\theta = n^2 r^{n-2}\cos n\theta$, and $\tfrac1{r^2}u_{\theta\theta} = -n^2 r^{n-2}\cos
n\theta$; the sum is zero. Indeed $r^n\cos n\theta = \operatorname{Re} z^n$.
:::

### Conformal maps

The matrix form of the Cauchy-Riemann equations says that a holomorphic map acts locally as a rotation-scaling. Such maps preserve angles, which is the geometric content of holomorphy.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-conformal}
#### Conformal map

A map $f$ between open subsets of the plane is **conformal** at $z_0$ if it preserves the angle (including its
orientation) between any two smooth curves through $z_0$. A holomorphic $f$ with $f'(z_0) \neq 0$ is conformal at
$z_0$: to first order it multiplies displacements by the complex number $f'(z_0)$, a rotation by $\arg f'(z_0)$
combined with a scaling by $|f'(z_0)|$. Conversely a continuously differentiable orientation-preserving conformal
map is holomorphic with non-vanishing derivative. A bijective holomorphic map with holomorphic inverse between two
domains is a **conformal equivalence**.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the map $z^2$ of the figure, which preserves angles away from the origin and doubles them there. The parabolas in the right panel of @fig-domain-colouring are its images of the grid.

::: {#exm-conformal-square}
#### $z \mapsto z^2$

The grid lines $\operatorname{Re} z = c$ and $\operatorname{Im} z = c$ are mapped by $z^2$ to the two families of
parabolas $u = c^2 - t^2$, $v = 2ct$ and $u = t^2 - c^2$, $v = 2tc$ of @fig-domain-colouring, which cross at right
angles wherever $z \neq 0$. At $z = 0$, where $f' = 0$, angles are doubled: the two half-axes, at angle $\pi$,
are both sent to the positive real axis.
:::

The second example is a Möbius transformation that maps the real line to the unit circle. These maps are the conformal equivalences of the disc and the half-plane.

::: {#exm-conformal-mobius}
#### A Möbius transformation

$f(z) = \dfrac{z - i}{z + i}$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{-i\}$ with $f'(z) = 2i/(z + i)^2 \neq 0$. For
real $x$, $|x - i| = |x + i|$, so $|f(x)| = 1$: the real axis is mapped into the unit circle, and the upper
half-plane (closer to $i$ than to $-i$) onto the open unit disc, conformally (@exr-conformal-mobius). Maps of the
form $(az + b)/(cz + d)$ with $ad - bc \neq 0$ are the Möbius transformations; they send circles and lines to
circles and lines.
:::

The third example is the exponential, conformal everywhere. It turns the rectangular grid into the polar grid, which explains why polar coordinates are orthogonal.

::: {#exm-conformal-exp}
#### The exponential as a conformal map

$e^z$ has $(e^z)' = e^z \neq 0$ everywhere, so it is conformal everywhere; it maps horizontal lines
$\operatorname{Im} z = y_0$ to rays of argument $y_0$ and vertical lines $\operatorname{Re} z = x_0$ to circles of
radius $e^{x_0}$: the rectangular grid becomes the polar grid, which is orthogonal too. The strip $0 <
\operatorname{Im} z < \pi$ is mapped onto the upper half-plane.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise verifies conformality of $z^2$ at one point by computing tangent vectors. Both tangents are rotated by the same angle and scaled by the same factor.

::: {#exr-conformal-angles}
#### Angles under $z^2$

Take the curves $\gamma_1(t) = 1 + i + t$ and $\gamma_2(t) = 1 + i + it$ through $z_0 = 1 + i$. Compute the
tangent vectors of their images under $f(z) = z^2$ at $f(z_0)$, check that they are orthogonal and that both are
rotated by $\arg f'(z_0) = \pi/4$ and scaled by $|f'(z_0)| = 2\sqrt2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(f\circ\gamma_k)'(0) = f'(z_0)\gamma_k'(0)$ by the chain rule, with $f'(z_0) = 2(1 + i) = 2\sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}$:
the images of the tangents $1$ and $i$ are $2 + 2i$ and $-2 + 2i$, orthogonal (dot product $-4 + 4 = 0$) and
each obtained from the original by the same rotation-scaling:

{{< sage exr-conformal-angles >}}
:::

The second exercise proves that the Cayley map is a conformal equivalence between the half-plane and the disc. The inverse map is found by solving a linear equation.

::: {#exr-conformal-mobius}
#### The Cayley map of the half-plane onto the disc

Show that $f(z) = (z - i)/(z + i)$ maps the upper half-plane bijectively onto the unit disc, find the inverse map,
and compute the images of $i$, $0$, $1$ and $\infty$ (as a limit).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|z - i| < |z + i|$ exactly when $z$ is closer to $i$ than to $-i$, that is, $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$, so $f$ maps
the half-plane into the disc; solving $w = (z - i)/(z + i)$ gives $z = i(1 + w)/(1 - w)$, which is defined for $|w|
< 1$ and maps the disc back into the half-plane ($\operatorname{Im} z = (1 - |w|^2)/|1 - w|^2 > 0$). $f(i) = 0$,
$f(0) = -1$, $f(1) = (1 - i)/(1 + i) = -i$, $f(z) \to 1$ as $|z| \to \infty$:

{{< sage exr-conformal-mobius >}}
:::

The third exercise generalises the angle doubling at a critical point. The order of vanishing of the derivative is the factor by which angles are multiplied.

::: {#exr-conformal-critical}
#### Angle multiplication at a critical point

Show that if $f$ is holomorphic near $z_0$ with $f'(z_0) = \dots = f^{(n-1)}(z_0) = 0$ and $f^{(n)}(z_0) \neq 0$
(assume the Taylor expansion of @def-taylor-series), then $f$ multiplies the angles between curves through $z_0$
by $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f(z) - f(z_0) = c(z - z_0)^n\bigl(1 + O(z - z_0)\bigr)$ with $c = f^{(n)}(z_0)/n! \neq 0$. Along a curve leaving
$z_0$ in the direction $e^{i\alpha}$, $f(z) - f(z_0) \approx c\,t^n e^{in\alpha}$ leaves $f(z_0)$ in the direction
$\arg c + n\alpha$. Two curves at angle $\beta - \alpha$ are mapped to curves at angle $n(\beta - \alpha)$:
$z^2$ at the origin doubles angles (@exm-conformal-square), $z^3$ triples them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

### Worked computations

The section closes with explicit instances of the Cauchy-Riemann equations. They cover the Cauchy-Riemann equations, harmonicity, the Jacobian and the zeros and poles of the plotted function.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-cauchy-riemann-examples}
#### Cauchy-Riemann checks

$z^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + i\,2xy$, $z^3$ and $e^z = e^x\cos y + ie^x\sin y$ satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations and
$\bar z$ violates them; $x^2 - y^2$ and $e^x\cos y$ are harmonic; the Jacobian of $z \mapsto z^2$ has determinant
$|2z|^2 = 4(x^2 + y^2)$ and orthogonal columns of equal length; and $(z - 1)/(z^2 + 1)$ has its zero at $1$ and
its poles at $\pm i$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example tests $z^3$ by substituting $z = x + iy$ and separating real and imaginary parts. The same
method decides holomorphy for any explicit function of $z$ and $\bar z$.

::: {#exm-cr-check-method}
#### Separating real and imaginary parts

For $f(z) = z^3$, $(x + iy)^3 = (x^3 - 3xy^2) + i(3x^2y - y^3)$, so $u = x^3 - 3xy^2$ and $v = 3x^2y - y^3$. Then
$u_x = 3x^2 - 3y^2 = v_y$ and $u_y = -6xy = -v_x$: the Cauchy-Riemann equations hold everywhere, and $f'(z) = u_x +
iv_x = 3(x^2 - y^2) + 6ixy = 3z^2$. For $g(z) = |z|^2 = x^2 + y^2$ instead, $u_x = 2x$, $v_y = 0$, $u_y = 2y$, $v_x
= 0$, and the equations hold only at $z = 0$.
:::

The second example reads the Jacobian of $z^2$ as a complex number. Orthogonal columns of equal length are the matrix form of conformality.

::: {#exm-cr-jacobian-structure}
#### The Jacobian as a complex number

For $z^2$ the Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix} 2x & -2y \\ 2y & 2x \end{pmatrix}$, the matrix of multiplication by
$2z$ in the sense of @exm-complex-matrices; its columns $(2x, 2y)$ and $(-2y, 2x)$ are orthogonal and of equal
length $2|z|$, which is the matrix form of conformality.
:::

The first exercise computes the Jacobian of the exponential and identifies it as a rotation-scaling. The rotation angle and the scale factor are the argument and the modulus of $e^z$.

::: {#exr-cr-exp-jacobian}
#### The Jacobian of the exponential

Compute the real Jacobian of $(x, y) \mapsto (e^x\cos y, e^x\sin y)$, check that it is $e^{2x}$ times a rotation
matrix, and identify the rotation angle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$J = e^x\begin{pmatrix} \cos y & -\sin y \\ \sin y & \cos y \end{pmatrix}$, with $\det J = e^{2x} = |e^z|^2$ and
$J^{\mathsf T}J = e^{2x}\,\mathbf 1$: a rotation by $y = \arg e^z$ scaled by $e^x = |e^z|$, as @def-conformal
predicts from $f' = e^z$:

{{< sage exr-cr-exp-jacobian >}}
:::

The second exercise proves in general that both parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic. Products of parts of $f$ are handled by looking at $f^2$.

::: {#exr-cr-harmonic-general}
#### Both parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic

Prove from the Cauchy-Riemann equations that $u$ and $v$ are harmonic whenever $f = u + iv$ is holomorphic with
$u, v$ twice continuously differentiable, and that $uv$ and $u^2 - v^2$ are harmonic too.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u_{xx} = (v_y)_x = v_{yx} = v_{xy} = (-u_y)_y = -u_{yy}$, using the symmetry of mixed partials, so $\Delta u = 0$;
similarly $\Delta v = 0$. $uv = \tfrac12\operatorname{Im}(f^2)$ and $u^2 - v^2 = \operatorname{Re}(f^2)$ are the
parts of the holomorphic function $f^2$, hence harmonic.
:::

The third exercise differentiates the inverse of a holomorphic map. The derivative of the logarithm follows once more, this time from the inverse function rule.

::: {#exr-cr-conformal-inverse}
#### The derivative of the inverse

Let $f$ be holomorphic and injective near $z_0$ with $f'(z_0) \neq 0$ and continuous inverse $g$. Show that $g$ is
complex differentiable at $w_0 = f(z_0)$ with $g'(w_0) = 1/f'(z_0)$, and apply it to $\operatorname{Log}$ as the
inverse of $e^z$ on a strip.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $w = f(z)$, $\dfrac{g(w) - g(w_0)}{w - w_0} = \dfrac{z - z_0}{f(z) - f(z_0)} \to \dfrac1{f'(z_0)}$ as $w \to
w_0$, since $z \to z_0$ by continuity of $g$. For $f = e^z$ on $-\pi < \operatorname{Im} z < \pi$ the inverse is
$\operatorname{Log}$, and $\operatorname{Log}' w = 1/e^{z} = 1/w$, confirming @exm-holomorphic-log.
:::

## Contour integration {#sec-contour-integration}

Contour integrals, Cauchy's theorem, Cauchy's integral formula and Liouville's theorem. Integrating a holomorphic
function along a curve depends only on the endpoints when the function has a primitive, and Cauchy's theorem says
that it always does locally; the integral formula then expresses a holomorphic function inside a closed curve by
its values on the curve, from which infinite differentiability, the Taylor series of @sec-residues and
Liouville's theorem follow.

![Contours. Left: the positively oriented unit circle $|z| = 1$, enclosing the pole of $1/z$ and not that of
$1/(z - 3)$. Right: the closed semicircular contour $[-R, R] + C_R$ used for real integrals, enclosing the pole
$i$ of $1/(1 + z^2)$ and the poles $e^{i\pi/4}$, $e^{3i\pi/4}$ of $1/(1 + z^4)$ in the upper half-plane, but not
$-i$. Generated by `figures/contours_poles.sage`.](figures/contours_poles.svg){#fig-contours-poles width=95%}

### Contours

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-contour}
#### Contour

A **contour** is a continuous, piecewise continuously differentiable map $\gamma : [a, b] \to \mathbb{C}$, together
with its orientation (the direction of increasing $t$); its image is also called the contour. It is **closed** if
$\gamma(a) = \gamma(b)$ and **simple** if it does not cross itself except possibly at the endpoints. A simple closed
contour separates the plane into a bounded **interior** and an unbounded exterior (the Jordan curve theorem), and
it is **positively oriented** if the interior lies to the left as one travels along it (counter-clockwise for a
circle). The **reversed contour** $-\gamma$ is $t \mapsto \gamma(a + b - t)$, and the **length** of $\gamma$ is
$L(\gamma) = \int_a^b |\gamma'(t)|\,dt$.
:::

The third exercise proves the invariance of length under reparametrisation and reversal. The semicircular contour of @exm-contour-semicircle is treated as an application.

::: {#exr-contour-reverse}
#### Reparametrisation

Show that the length of a contour does not change under a reparametrisation $t = \phi(s)$ with $\phi' > 0$, nor
under reversal, and that the semicircular contour of @exm-contour-semicircle has length $2R + \pi R$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}

substitution rule of @sec-riemann-integral; reversal is $\phi(s) = a + b - s$ with $|\phi'| = 1$. The segment has
length $2R$ and the half-circle $\pi R$.
:::

### Contour integrals

With contours defined, we can integrate along them. The contour integral is the natural generalisation of the Riemann integral, and the existence of a primitive makes it depend only on the endpoints.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-contour-integral}
#### Contour integral

The **contour integral** of a continuous $f$ along $\gamma : [a, b] \to \mathbb{C}$ is
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz = \int_a^b f\bigl(\gamma(t)\bigr)\,\gamma'(t)\,dt,$$
a complex number computed as two real Riemann integrals (@sec-riemann-integral). It is unchanged by
orientation-preserving reparametrisation, changes sign under reversal, $\int_{-\gamma} f = -\int_\gamma f$, and
obeys the **ML estimate** $\bigl|\int_\gamma f\,dz\bigr| \leq M L(\gamma)$ when $|f| \leq M$ on $\gamma$. If $f =
F'$ for a holomorphic $F$ (a **primitive**) on an open set containing $\gamma$, then $\int_\gamma f\,dz =
F(\gamma(b)) - F(\gamma(a))$, which vanishes for closed $\gamma$. A closed contour integral is written $\oint_\gamma$.
:::

The first example is the computation on which everything else rests. Only $1/z$ has a non-zero integral around the circle, because only $1/z$ lacks a single-valued primitive.

::: {#exm-integral-powers-circle}
#### Powers of $z$ around the circle

On $\gamma(t) = e^{it}$, $\oint z^n\,dz = \int_0^{2\pi} e^{int}\,ie^{it}\,dt = i\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(n+1)t}\,dt$,
which is $2\pi i$ for $n = -1$ and $0$ for every other integer $n$ (@prp-circle-integrals): for $n \neq -1$, $z^n$
has the primitive $z^{n+1}/(n + 1)$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, while $1/z$ has none there (its would-be
primitive $\log z$ is many-valued).
:::

The second example uses a primitive to evaluate an integral without choosing a path. Any path from $0$ to $1 + i$ gives the same answer.

::: {#exm-integral-primitive}
#### Using a primitive

$\int_\gamma z^2\,dz$ from $0$ to $1 + i$ equals $(1 + i)^3/3 = (-2 + 2i)/3$ along the straight segment, along the
parabola $t + it^2$, or along any other path, since $z^3/3$ is a primitive on all of $\mathbb{C}$
(@prp-circle-integrals checks the segment).

The third example shows path dependence for a non-holomorphic integrand. The two paths give different values, so no primitive can exist.

::: {#exm-integral-path-dependence}
#### A path-dependent integral

$\int \bar z\,dz$ from $0$ to $1 + i$ is $\int_0^1 (t - it)(1 + i)\,dt = 1$ along the segment but $\int_0^1 (t -
it^2)(1 + 2it)\,dt = 1 + \tfrac i3$ along the parabola $t + it^2$: $\bar z$ has no primitive, in keeping with its
failure to be holomorphic (@exr-integral-segment).
:::

The second exercise applies the ML estimate to a concrete integral. The bound is crude, but the technique is the one that discards arcs at infinity.

::: {#exr-integral-ml}
#### An ML estimate

Bound $\bigl|\oint_{|z| = 2} e^z/(z^2 + 1)\,dz\bigr|$ with the ML estimate, and compare with the exact value $2\pi
i\sin 1$ that @thm-residue will give.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $|z| = 2$, $|e^z| = e^{\operatorname{Re} z} \leq e^2$ and $|z^2 + 1| \geq |z|^2 - 1 = 3$ (@exm-modulus-reverse-triangle),
so $M = e^2/3$, $L = 4\pi$ and the bound is $4\pi e^2/3 \approx 30.9$; the exact modulus is $2\pi\sin 1 \approx 5.
29$. The estimate is crude but it is all one needs to discard large arcs.
:::

### Cauchy's theorem

The vanishing of closed integrals of functions with a primitive is now promoted to a theorem about all holomorphic functions. Cauchy's theorem is the central result of complex analysis.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-cauchy}
#### Cauchy's theorem

Let $\gamma$ be a simple closed contour and $f$ holomorphic on an open set containing $\gamma$ and its interior.
Then
$$\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 0.$$
More generally, if $f$ is holomorphic on a domain $D$ and $\gamma$ can be continuously deformed within $D$ to
another closed contour $\gamma'$ (or to a point), then $\oint_\gamma f\,dz = \oint_{\gamma'} f\,dz$ (or $0$):
closed contour integrals of holomorphic functions depend only on the deformation class of the contour within the
domain of holomorphy. Equivalently, a holomorphic function on a disc has a primitive there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example applies the theorem to entire functions, where the hypothesis is automatic. Every closed contour integral of a polynomial or of the exponential vanishes.

::: {#exm-cauchy-entire}
#### Entire functions

$\oint_\gamma e^z\,dz = \oint_\gamma \cos z\,dz = \oint_\gamma p(z)\,dz = 0$ for every closed contour $\gamma$ and
polynomial $p$: entire functions have entire primitives ($e^z$, $\sin z$, the term-by-term primitive of $p$).
:::

The second example contrasts a contour that does not enclose the singularity with one that does. The hypothesis of the theorem concerns the interior of the contour, not only the contour itself.

::: {#exm-cauchy-pole-outside}
#### A pole outside the contour

$1/(z - 3)$ is holomorphic on the disc $|z| < 3$, which contains the unit circle and its interior, so
$\oint_{|z|=1} dz/(z - 3) = 0$ (@fig-contours-poles, @prp-circle-integrals). The same integral over $|z| = 4$ is
$2\pi i$: the value depends on whether the contour encloses the singularity.
:::

The third example illustrates the deformation form of the theorem. The integral of $1/z$ is the same over every contour that winds once around the origin.

::: {#exm-cauchy-deformation}
#### Deforming a contour

$\oint dz/z$ is $2\pi i$ over any circle around the origin, of any radius, and over the boundary of any square
containing $0$, since each of these contours deforms into the unit circle within $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$;
only the point $0$ obstructs shrinking the contour to a point.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for two vanishing results without computation. The second one shows that winding around a singularity is not by itself an obstruction.

::: {#exr-cauchy-polynomial}
#### Closed integrals of polynomials and of $1/z^2$

Show without computing that $\oint_\gamma (z^5 - 3z + 2)\,dz = 0$ for every closed $\gamma$, and that
$\oint_\gamma dz/z^2 = 0$ for every closed $\gamma$ not passing through $0$, even one that winds around $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The polynomial is entire, so Cauchy's theorem applies; or note that $z^6/6 - 3z^2/2 + 2z$ is a primitive. $1/z^2$
has the single-valued primitive $-1/z$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, so every closed integral vanishes
regardless of winding; the obstruction for $1/z$ is specifically that its primitive $\log z$ is many-valued.
:::

The second exercise evaluates an integral over a square by deforming it to a circle. The justification is that the deformation avoids the only singularity.

::: {#exr-cauchy-deform}
#### From a square to a circle

Evaluate $\oint_\gamma \dfrac{dz}{z}$ over the boundary $\gamma$ of the square with vertices $\pm 2 \pm 2i$ by
deforming it to a circle, and explain why the deformation is allowed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The square can be shrunk radially onto the unit circle without crossing $0$, the only point where $1/z$ is not
holomorphic, so the integral equals $\oint_{|z|=1} dz/z = 2\pi i$. A direct computation over the four sides would
give four arctangent integrals adding up to the same $2\pi i$.
:::

The third exercise analyses a wrong answer produced by a symbolic integrator. The error is a branch cut crossed by the primitive, exactly the issue of @def-branch.

::: {#exr-cauchy-maxima-pitfall}
#### A wrong answer from a symbolic integrator

Sage's symbolic `integrate` of the parametrised form of $\oint_{|z| = 1} dz/(z - 3)$ returns $-2\pi i$, whereas
Cauchy's theorem gives $0$ and numerical integration agrees. Find the error.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The integrator uses the primitive $\log(e^{it} - 3)$ and evaluates it at the endpoints $t = 0, 2\pi$ with the
principal branch. The point $e^{it} - 3$ starts at $-2$, on the cut, and circles it: the principal argument is
near $+\pi$ just after $t = 0$ and near $-\pi$ just before $t = 2\pi$, so the endpoint difference is $-2\pi i$
instead of the $0$ that a branch continuous along the path would give. A primitive must be single-valued and
continuous along the whole contour to be used; @def-branch is not a formality:

{{< sage exr-cauchy-maxima-pitfall >}}
:::

### Cauchy's integral formula

Cauchy's theorem applied to $f(z)/(z - z_0)$ gives a formula for the values of a holomorphic function inside a contour. Differentiating under the integral gives all derivatives at once.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-cauchy-integral-formula}
#### Cauchy's integral formula

Let $\gamma$ be a positively oriented simple closed contour and $f$ holomorphic on an open set containing $\gamma$
and its interior. Then for every $z_0$ in the interior
$$f(z_0) = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\,dz, \qquad f^{(n)}(z_0) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma
\frac{f(z)}{(z - z_0)^{n+1}}\,dz.$$
In particular a holomorphic function is infinitely complex differentiable, and on a disc of radius $r$ about
$z_0$ on which $|f| \leq M$ it satisfies the **Cauchy estimates** $|f^{(n)}(z_0)| \leq n!\,M/r^n$.
:::

M / R^n in interval arithmetic.

The second example specialises the formula to a circle and reads it as an average. The mean value property of harmonic functions follows by taking real parts.

::: {#exm-cif-mean-value}
#### The mean value property

With $\gamma(t) = z_0 + re^{it}$, $dz/(z - z_0) = i\,dt$ and the formula reads $f(z_0) = \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
f(z_0 + re^{it})\,dt$: the value at the centre is the average over any circle, for the function and hence for its
harmonic real and imaginary parts (@exr-harmonic-mean-value).
:::

The third example draws the qualitative conclusion from the formula. Boundary values control all the derivatives inside, and the Cauchy estimates make this control quantitative.

::: {#exm-cif-derivative-from-values}
#### Derivatives from boundary values

The formula for $f^{(n)}$ shows that the boundary values of a holomorphic function determine all its derivatives
inside; a holomorphic function that is small on a circle has small derivatives at the centre, which is what the
Cauchy estimates quantify and what @cor-liouville exploits.
:::

$\pi$ lies inside $|z| = 4$, so the first is $2\pi i\cos\pi = -2\pi i$; it lies outside $|z| = 1$, where the
integrand is holomorphic, so the second is $0$. Sage computes the first as a residue (@def-residue) and checks it

#### The derivative formula

Evaluate $\oint_{|z| = 1} \dfrac{e^{2z}}{z^3}\,dz$ and $\oint_{|z| = 2} \dfrac{z^2}{(z - 1)^2}\,dz$.

$2\pi i\,f'(1) = 4\pi i$:

The third exercise derives the Cauchy estimates and tests their sharpness on the exponential. The bound is weak, but it is what Liouville's theorem needs.

::: {#exr-cif-estimates}
#### The Cauchy estimates

Derive $|f^{(n)}(z_0)| \leq n!\,M/r^n$ from the derivative formula and the ML estimate, and apply it to $f = e^z$
at $z_0 = 0$ with $r = 1$ and $n = 10$ to bound $1 = f^{(10)}(0)$ (how good is the bound?).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the circle $|z - z_0| = r$ the integrand has modulus at most $M/r^{n+1}$ and the length is $2\pi r$, so
$|f^{(n)}(z_0)| \leq \frac{n!}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{M}{r^{n+1}}\cdot 2\pi r = n!\,M/r^n$. For $e^z$ on $|z| = 1$, $M =
e$ and the bound is $10!\,e \approx 9.9\times 10^6$ for a quantity equal to $1$: the estimate is far from sharp but
suffices for @cor-liouville.
:::

### Liouville's theorem

The Cauchy estimates have an immediate consequence for functions holomorphic on the whole plane. Growth at infinity controls the degree, and boundedness forces constancy.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#cor-liouville}
#### Liouville's theorem

A bounded entire function is constant. More generally an entire function with $|f(z)| \leq C(1 + |z|)^n$ for all
$z$ is a polynomial of degree at most $n$. (From the Cauchy estimates with $r \to \infty$: every derivative of
order $> n$ vanishes.)
:::

::: {#exm-liouville-exp}
#### $e^z$, $\cos z$, $\sin z$ are unbounded

They are entire and non-constant, so by Liouville's theorem they cannot be bounded: indeed $|e^x| \to \infty$ and
$\cos(iy) = \cosh y \to \infty$ (@exm-exp-trig-complex). A bounded non-constant function on $\mathbb{R}$ like
$\cos x$ extends to an entire function only at the price of unboundedness off the real axis.
:::

The second example is the classical proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra. A polynomial without zeros would have a bounded entire reciprocal.

::: {#exm-liouville-fta}
#### The fundamental theorem of algebra

If a non-constant polynomial $p$ had no zero, $1/p$ would be entire and bounded (it tends to $0$ at infinity),
hence constant: a contradiction. So every non-constant polynomial has a complex root, and by repeated division
$p(z) = c\prod_k (z - z_k)$ (@exr-liouville-fta).
:::

The third example illustrates the growth version of the theorem. In particular no entire function can behave like the square root at infinity.

::: {#exm-liouville-rational}
#### Entire functions of polynomial growth

$f$ entire with $|f(z)| \leq C|z|^2$ for large $|z|$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$; an entire function
bounded by a constant times $\sqrt{|z|}$ is constant. There is no entire function behaving like $\sqrt z$ at
infinity (the square root has a branch point, @exm-branch-sqrt).
:::
