The first exercise examines the growth of the sine along lines. Boundedness on each horizontal line does not contradict the theorem, which needs a bound on the whole plane.

::: {#exr-liouville-sin}
#### Boundedness on lines

Show that $\sin z$ is bounded on every horizontal line but unbounded on every vertical line, and reconcile this
with Liouville's theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\sin(x + iy)|^2 = \sin^2 x + \sinh^2 y$ (expand $\sin(x + iy) = \sin x\cosh y + i\cos x\sinh y$ and use
$\cosh^2 - \sinh^2 = 1$). For fixed $y$ it is at most $1 + \sinh^2 y$; for fixed $x$ it grows like $e^{2|y|}/4$.
Boundedness on lines, or on any half-plane, does not contradict Liouville, which needs a bound on the whole plane.
:::

The second exercise completes the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra. The bound on $1/p$ uses compactness of discs, from @sec-compact-connected.

::: {#exr-liouville-fta}
#### Factorising a polynomial completely

Complete the argument of @exm-liouville-fta: show that $1/p$ is bounded when $p$ has no zeros, and that a
polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $p(z) = a_n z^n + \dots + a_0$ with $a_n \neq 0$, $|p(z)| \geq |a_n||z|^n - \sum_{k<n}|a_k||z|^k \geq
\tfrac12|a_n||z|^n$ for $|z| \geq R$ large, so $|1/p| \leq 2/(|a_n|R^n)$ there; on the compact disc $|z| \leq R$
the continuous function $1/p$ is bounded (@sec-compact-connected). Hence $1/p$ is bounded, entire if $p$ has no
zero, thus constant, which is absurd for $n \geq 1$. Given a root $z_1$, $p(z) = (z - z_1)q(z)$ with $\deg q = n -
1$ by polynomial division, and induction on the degree gives $n$ roots with multiplicity.
:::

The third exercise proves the growth version of the theorem using the Taylor series of the next section. Only finitely many Taylor coefficients can survive the estimates.

::: {#exr-liouville-bounded-growth}
#### Growth and degree

Prove the general form of Liouville's theorem: an entire $f$ with $|f(z)| \leq C(1 + |z|)^n$ is a polynomial of
degree at most $n$. (Apply the Cauchy estimates on circles of radius $r \to \infty$ and use the Taylor series of
@def-taylor-series.)
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $|z| = r$, $|f| \leq C(1 + r)^n$, so $|f^{(k)}(0)| \leq k!\,C(1 + r)^n/r^k \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$ for $k >
n$. Hence all Taylor coefficients $f^{(k)}(0)/k!$ with $k > n$ vanish, and the Taylor series of $f$ at $0$, which
converges to $f$ on the whole plane, is a polynomial of degree at most $n$. For $n = 0$ this is the bounded case.
:::

### Worked computations

The section closes with explicit circle integrals of powers of $z$, of $1/(z - 3)$ and of $e^z/z$ and $e^z/z^2$. They are the computations behind @exm-integral-powers-circle, @exm-cauchy-pole-outside and @exm-cif-exp.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-circle-integrals}
#### Circle integrals

$\oint_{|z|=1} z^n\,dz = 2\pi i$ for $n = -1$ and $0$ for $n \in \{-3, \dots, 3\}\setminus\{-1\}$; $\oint_{|z|=1}
dz/(z - 3) = 0$ (the Taylor series of $1/(z - 3)$ on $|z| < 3$ has no $1/z$ term, and the parametrised integral
vanishes numerically); the residues of $e^z/z$ and $e^z/z^2$ at $0$ are both $1$, so that both circle integrals
equal $2\pi i$, the parametrised integral of $e^z/z$ agreeing to $10^{-9}$; and $\int_0^{1+i} z^2\,dz = (1 +
i)^3/3$ along the segment.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example evaluates the circle integrals directly from the parametrisation of the circle. For the powers
of $z$ this is an elementary integral, and for $e^z/z$ the Taylor series of the exponential reduces it to the same
computation.

::: {#exm-circle-check-method}
#### Integrating along the parametrised circle

With $z = e^{it}$, $dz = ie^{it}dt$, $\oint_{|z|=1} z^n\,dz = i\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(n+1)t}\,dt$, which is $2\pi i$ for
$n = -1$ and $0$ otherwise. For $e^z/z$, $\oint_{|z|=1} \frac{e^z}{z}\,dz = i\int_0^{2\pi} e^{e^{it}}\,dt =
i\sum_{k \geq 0}\frac{1}{k!}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{ikt}\,dt = 2\pi i$, the uniformly convergent series being integrated
term by term: only $k = 0$ survives, in agreement with the residue $1$ of $e^z/z$ at $0$.
:::

The second example reads the circle integrals as orthogonality relations. The Laurent coefficients of the next section are Fourier coefficients in disguise.

::: {#exm-circle-fourier-orthogonality}
#### Circle integrals as Fourier orthogonality

$\oint_{|z|=1} z^n\,dz = i\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(n+1)t}\,dt$ is $2\pi i$ times the Kronecker delta $\delta_{n, -1}$:
the vanishing of the circle integrals of $z^n$ is the orthogonality of the exponentials $e^{imt}$ on $[0, 2\pi]$,
and the coefficient extraction of @def-laurent-series is a Fourier coefficient computation.
:::

The second exercise shows that the radius of the circle never matters. For $n = -1$ this is the deformation form of Cauchy's theorem.

::: {#exr-circle-radius}
#### Independence of the radius

Show by direct parametrisation that $\oint_{|z| = r} z^n\,dz$ does not depend on $r > 0$ for any integer $n$, and
explain the result for $n \leq -2$ and for $n = -1$ by @thm-cauchy.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\oint_{|z|=r} z^n\,dz = ir^{n+1}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(n+1)t}\,dt$, which is $0$ for $n \neq -1$ (whatever $r$) and
$2\pi i$ for $n = -1$ (the factor $r^0 = 1$). For $n \neq -1$ the function has a primitive on
$\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$; for $n = -1$ the circles of different radii deform into one another within
$\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, so the integrals agree even though they are non-zero.
:::

:::

The third exercise derives the orthogonality of the exponentials from the circle integrals. The coefficient formula at the end is the one used for Laurent series.

::: {#exr-circle-fourier}
#### Orthogonality of the Fourier modes

Deduce from @prp-circle-integrals that $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{imt}e^{-int}\,dt = 2\pi\delta_{mn}$ for integers $m, n$,
and use it to extract the coefficients of a trigonometric polynomial $p(t) = \sum_{|k| \leq N} c_k e^{ikt}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $z = e^{it}$, $e^{i(m - n)t}\,dt = z^{m - n}\,dz/(iz) = -i z^{m - n - 1}\,dz$, whose circle integral is
$-i\cdot 2\pi i\,\delta_{m - n - 1, -1} = 2\pi\delta_{mn}$. Multiplying $p$ by $e^{-int}$ and integrating kills
every term except $k = n$: $c_n = \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} p(t)e^{-int}\,dt$, the Fourier coefficient formula
in the form that @def-laurent-series uses for the Laurent coefficients.
:::

## Series and residues {#sec-residues}

Taylor and Laurent series, poles, the residue theorem and real integrals computed by residues. Cauchy's integral
formula expands a holomorphic function in a power series on every disc where it is holomorphic, and in a
two-sided series on every annulus; the coefficient of $1/(z - z_0)$ in the latter, the residue, is all that a
closed contour integral sees, and the residue theorem turns the evaluation of integrals into algebra.

![Laurent series of $f(z) = 1/((z - 1)(z - 2))$. Left: the three regions $|z| < 1$, $1 < |z| < 2$ and $|z| > 2$ on
which $f$ has three different expansions, separated by circles through the poles. Right: the error
$|S_N(z) - f(z)|$ of the partial sums of the annulus expansion at $z = 1.5i$, decreasing geometrically with $N$.
Generated by `figures/laurent_series.sage`.](figures/laurent_series.svg){#fig-laurent-series width=90%}

{{< interactive laurent_series 480 >}}

### Taylor series

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-taylor-series}
#### Taylor series

A **power series** about $z_0$ is $\sum_{n \geq 0} a_n (z - z_0)^n$; it converges absolutely for $|z - z_0| < R$ and
diverges for $|z - z_0| > R$, where $R \in [0, \infty]$ is the **radius of convergence**, $1/R = \limsup |
a_n|^{1/n}$ (the root test of @sec-series). Inside the disc of convergence the sum is holomorphic and may be
differentiated term by term. Conversely, if $f$ is holomorphic on the disc $|z - z_0| < R$, then on that disc
$$f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{f^{(n)}(z_0)}{n!}(z - z_0)^n,$$
its **Taylor series**, with coefficients given by Cauchy's integral formula; the radius of convergence is at least
the distance from $z_0$ to the nearest point where $f$ fails to be holomorphic.
:::

The second example explains a radius of convergence that is invisible from the real line. The function is smooth
and bounded on $\mathbb{R}$, yet its series stops converging at $|x| = 1$ because of poles off the axis.

::: {#exm-taylor-radius-poles}
#### Why $1/(1 + x^2)$ has radius $1$

$1/(1 + z^2) = \sum (-1)^n z^{2n}$ has radius of convergence $1$, although the function is smooth and bounded on
the whole real line: the poles at $\pm i$ (@fig-domain-colouring) are at distance $1$ from the origin. The complex
plane explains a phenomenon that is mysterious in real analysis.
:::

The second exercise asks for radii of convergence from the geometry alone. Locating the nearest singularity is
faster than any test on the coefficients.

::: {#exr-taylor-radius}
#### Radii from singularities

Without computing coefficients, find the radius of convergence of the Taylor series about $z_0 = 0$ and about
$z_0 = 1$ of $f(z) = 1/(z^2 + 4)$, and about $z_0 = 1$ of $\operatorname{Log} z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The poles are at $\pm 2i$: distance $2$ from $0$ and $\sqrt5$ from $1$, so $R = 2$ and $R = \sqrt5$. The principal
logarithm is holomorphic on the slit plane, and the nearest point of the cut to $1$ is $0$, at distance $1$:
$R = 1$, in agreement with the series of $\operatorname{Log}(1 + z)$ in @exm-taylor-standard.
:::

The third exercise derives the Taylor expansion from the integral formula. The geometric series does the work,
and the Cauchy estimates reappear as bounds on the coefficients.

::: {#exr-taylor-cauchy-estimates}
#### The Taylor expansion from the integral formula

Derive the Taylor series of $f$ on $|z - z_0| < r$ by expanding $\frac1{w - z} = \frac1{(w - z_0)}\cdot\frac1{1 -
(z - z_0)/(w - z_0)}$ in Cauchy's formula over $|w - z_0| = r$, and deduce $|a_n| \leq M/r^n$ when $|f| \leq M$
on the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $|z - z_0| < r = |w - z_0|$ the geometric series $\sum_n (z - z_0)^n/(w - z_0)^{n+1}$ converges uniformly in
$w$ on the circle, so it may be integrated term by term: $f(z) = \sum_n (z - z_0)^n\cdot\frac1{2\pi i}\oint
\frac{f(w)\,dw}{(w - z_0)^{n+1}}$, which identifies $a_n$ with the circle integral. The ML estimate on the
integral gives $|a_n| \leq \frac1{2\pi}\cdot\frac{M}{r^{n+1}}\cdot 2\pi r = M/r^n$.
:::

### Laurent series

Taylor series describe a function near a point where it is holomorphic. Near a singular point, or on a ring
between two singularities, one needs negative powers as well, and the resulting two-sided expansion is unique on
each annulus.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-laurent-series}
#### Laurent series

If $f$ is holomorphic on the annulus $r < |z - z_0| < R$, then there it equals its **Laurent series**
$$f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n (z - z_0)^n, \qquad a_n = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z - z_0| = \rho} \frac{f(z)}{(z -
z_0)^{n+1}}\,dz \quad (r < \rho < R),$$
converging absolutely on the annulus; the coefficients are unique, and the part with $n < 0$ is the **principal
part**. The same function has different Laurent series on different annuli about the same point.
:::

::: {#exm-laurent-three-regions}
#### Three expansions of one function

$f(z) = \dfrac1{(z - 1)(z - 2)} = \dfrac1{z - 2} - \dfrac1{z - 1}$ (@fig-laurent-series). On $|z| < 1$ both terms
are geometric series in $z$: $f = \sum_n (1 - 2^{-n-1}) z^n$, a Taylor series. On $1 < |z| < 2$ expand $1/(z - 2)$
in $z/2$ and $1/(z - 1)$ in $1/z$: $f = -\sum_{n \geq 0} z^n/2^{n+1} - \sum_{n \geq 1} z^{-n}$, with infinitely
many negative powers. On $|z| > 2$ both are expanded in $1/z$: $f = \sum_{n \geq 2}(2^{n-1} - 1)z^{-n}$.
:::

::: {#exm-laurent-essential}
#### $e^{1/z}$

Substituting $1/z$ into the exponential series, $e^{1/z} = \sum_{n \geq 0} z^{-n}/n!$ on $0 < |z| < \infty$: the
principal part is infinite, and $a_{-1} = 1$. The partial sums shown in the interactive version of
@fig-laurent-series are the analogous sums for the function of @exm-laurent-three-regions.

The third example divides one series by another. The leading term of the result is a simple pole, and the next
terms are found by matching coefficients.

::: {#exm-laurent-cosecant}
#### $1/\sin z$

From $\sin z = z - z^3/6 + z^5/120 - \dots$, $\dfrac1{\sin z} = \dfrac1z\cdot\dfrac1{1 - z^2/6 + z^4/120 - \dots} =
\dfrac1z + \dfrac z6 + \dfrac{7z^3}{360} + \dots$ on $0 < |z| < \pi$ (the next zeros of $\sin$ are at $\pm\pi$).
The principal part is $1/z$ (@prp-residue-integrals checks the three terms).
:::

The third exercise proves the uniqueness of the Laurent coefficients from the circle integrals. The orthogonality
of @exr-circle-fourier is exactly what is needed.

::: {#exr-laurent-uniqueness}
#### Uniqueness of the coefficients

Show that if $f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} b_n (z - z_0)^n$ on an annulus, with the series converging uniformly
on each circle inside it, then $b_n$ equals the coefficient $a_n$ of @def-laurent-series.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Multiply by $(z - z_0)^{-m-1}$ and integrate over a circle in the annulus, exchanging sum and integral by uniform
convergence: $\oint f(z)(z - z_0)^{-m-1}\,dz = \sum_n b_n\oint (z - z_0)^{n-m-1}\,dz = 2\pi i\,b_m$ by
@prp-circle-integrals (only $n = m$ survives). Hence $b_m = a_m$: however a Laurent expansion is found, by
partial fractions, substitution or division, it is the Laurent expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (oracle, 5 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.LaurentSeries.circle_zpow`; Test (oracle, 5 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.LaurentSeries.laurent_coeff`.

**Lean.**

### Isolated singularities

A point where a function is not defined but around which it is holomorphic is classified by its principal part.
Three cases arise, from the harmless to the wild, and the classification decides what the residue theorem can do.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-isolated-singularity}
#### Isolated singularity

A point $z_0$ is an **isolated singularity** of $f$ if $f$ is holomorphic on a punctured disc $0 < |z - z_0| < r$
but not defined (or not holomorphic) at $z_0$. According to the principal part of the Laurent series on the
punctured disc, the singularity is **removable** (no negative powers: $f$ extends holomorphically to $z_0$), a
**pole of order** $m$ (finitely many, the lowest being $a_{-m}(z - z_0)^{-m}$ with $a_{-m} \neq 0$; then $|f(z)|
\to \infty$ as $z \to z_0$), or **essential** (infinitely many). A function holomorphic on a domain except for
poles is **meromorphic**; a simple pole is one of order $1$.
:::

The second exercise finds the order of a pole by combining factors. Orders of poles add under multiplication and
cancel against orders of zeros.

::: {#exr-singularity-order}
#### Orders of poles

Find the order of the pole at $0$ of $\dfrac1{z^2\sin z}$, of $\dfrac{\sin z}{z^3}$, and of $\dfrac{e^z -
1}{z^2}$, and the order of the pole of $\dfrac1{(z^2 + 1)^3}$ at $i$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sin z$ has a simple zero at $0$, so $1/(z^2\sin z)$ has a pole of order $3$; $\sin z/z^3 = z^{-2} - 1/6 + \dots$
has order $2$; $(e^z - 1)/z^2 = z^{-1} + 1/2 + \dots$ has order $1$. $(z^2 + 1)^3 = (z - i)^3(z + i)^3$ and $(z +
i)^{-3}$ is holomorphic near $i$, so the pole has order $3$.
:::

The third exercise explores the wild behaviour at an essential singularity. The equation $e^{1/z} = w$ has
infinitely many solutions in every punctured neighbourhood of $0$.

::: {#exr-singularity-casorati}
#### Values near an essential singularity

Show that for every $w \neq 0$ and every $\epsilon > 0$ the equation $e^{1/z} = w$ has infinitely many solutions
with $0 < |z| < \epsilon$, and that $w = 0$ is never attained.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{1/z} = w$ means $1/z \in \log w = \{\operatorname{Log} w + 2\pi i k\}$, so $z_k = 1/(\operatorname{Log} w +
2\pi i k)$, and $|z_k| \to 0$ as $k \to \pm\infty$: infinitely many solutions lie in every punctured disc. The
exponential never vanishes (@exr-exp-surjective), so $0$ is the one exceptional value. This is Picard's theorem
for this function.
:::

### Residues

Of all the Laurent coefficients, one has a special role. The coefficient of $1/(z - z_0)$ is the only one that a
closed contour integral around $z_0$ detects, and it can be computed without finding the whole series.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-residue}
#### Residue

The **residue** of $f$ at an isolated singularity $z_0$ is the coefficient $a_{-1}$ of its Laurent series on a
punctured disc about $z_0$, $\operatorname{Res}_{z = z_0} f = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint f(z)\,dz$ over a small positively
oriented circle. At a simple pole $\operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f = \lim_{z \to z_0}(z - z_0)f(z)$, and if $f = g/h$
with $g(z_0) \neq 0$, $h(z_0) = 0$, $h'(z_0) \neq 0$, then $\operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f = g(z_0)/h'(z_0)$; at a
pole of order $m$,
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z = z_0} f = \frac1{(m - 1)!}\lim_{z \to z_0}\frac{d^{m-1}}{dz^{m-1}}\Bigl[(z - z_0)^m f(z)\Bigr].$$
:::

The third example looks at the point at infinity. The sum of all residues of a rational function, including the
one at infinity, vanishes, which gives a check on any residue computation.

::: {#exm-residue-infinity}
#### The residue at infinity

For a function holomorphic for $|z| > R$, the residue at infinity is $\operatorname{Res}_\infty f = -\frac1{2\pi
i}\oint_{|z| = \rho} f\,dz$ for $\rho > R$, the coefficient $-a_{-1}$ of the Laurent series at infinity. For $f =
1/((z - 1)(z - 2)) = z^{-2} + \dots$ it is $0$, and indeed $-1 + 1 + 0 = 0$: the residues of a rational function,
including infinity, always sum to zero (@exr-residue-infinity).
:::

= \Bigl(1 - \dfrac1{z^2}\Bigr)\Big|_1 = 0$. The residue at infinity is $-1$ (the function behaves as $1/z$), and
$1 + 0 - 1 = 0$:

The second exercise derives the general formula for a pole of order $m$ from the Laurent series. The derivative
of order $m - 1$ isolates exactly the coefficient $a_{-1}$.

::: {#exr-residue-formula}
#### The formula for a pole of order $m$

Derive the formula for $\operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f$ at a pole of order $m$ from the Laurent series, and the
quotient rule $g(z_0)/h'(z_0)$ at a simple pole.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(z - z_0)^m f(z) = a_{-m} + \dots + a_{-1}(z - z_0)^{m-1} + a_0 (z - z_0)^m + \dots$ is holomorphic near $z_0$;
its $(m - 1)$-st derivative at $z_0$ is $(m - 1)!\,a_{-1}$. For $f = g/h$ with a simple zero of $h$, $(z -
z_0)f(z) = g(z)\cdot\dfrac{z - z_0}{h(z) - h(z_0)} \to g(z_0)/h'(z_0)$.
:::

The third exercise applies the quotient rule to the poles of $1/(1 + z^4)$. Writing the roots as exponentials
keeps the computation short and shows that the residues come in conjugate pairs.

::: {#exr-residue-quotient}
#### Residues of $1/(1 + z^4)$

Find the four poles of $1/(1 + z^4)$ and their residues with the quotient rule, and show that the two residues in
the upper half-plane sum to $-\dfrac{i}{2\sqrt2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The poles are $z_k = e^{i\pi(2k + 1)/4}$, and $\operatorname{Res}_{z_k} = 1/(4z_k^3) = -z_k/4$ (since $z_k^4 = -
1$). In the upper half-plane, $-\tfrac14(e^{i\pi/4} + e^{3i\pi/4}) = -\tfrac14\cdot 2i\sin(\pi/4)\cdot
e^{i\pi/2}/i$; more simply, $e^{i\pi/4} + e^{3i\pi/4} = i\sqrt2$, so the sum is $-i\sqrt2/4 = -i/(2\sqrt2)$. Then
$2\pi i\cdot(-i/(2\sqrt2)) = \pi/\sqrt2$, the integral of @prp-residue-integrals.
:::

### The residue theorem

Cauchy's theorem for a function with finitely many isolated singularities inside the contour is the residue
theorem. The contour is shrunk onto small circles around the singularities, each contributing $2\pi i$ times its
residue.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-residue}
#### Residue theorem

Let $\gamma$ be a positively oriented simple closed contour and $f$ holomorphic on an open set containing $\gamma$
and its interior except at finitely many points $z_1, \dots, z_k$ inside $\gamma$. Then
$$\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i\sum_{j = 1}^k \operatorname{Res}_{z = z_j} f.$$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The first example is the integral of the figure's function over a circle enclosing both poles. The two residues
cancel, so the integral vanishes, as the behaviour at infinity also predicts.

::: {#exm-residue-theorem-two-poles}
#### Both poles enclosed

$\oint_{|z| = 3}\dfrac{dz}{(z - 1)(z - 2)} = 2\pi i(-1 + 1) = 0$, while $\oint_{|z| = 1.5}$ encloses only $z = 1$
and equals $-2\pi i$. The first result also follows from the Laurent series at infinity, $f = z^{-2} + \dots$,
which has no $1/z$ term.
:::

The second example is the prototype of a real integral evaluated by residues. The semicircular contour of
@fig-contours-poles encloses one pole, and the arc contributes nothing in the limit.

::: {#exm-residue-theorem-real-integral}
#### $\int_{-\infty}^\infty dx/(1 + x^2) = \pi$

Over the contour $[-R, R] + C_R$ of @exm-contour-semicircle with $R > 1$, the only enclosed pole of $1/(1 + z^2)$ is
$i$, with residue $-i/2$, so the contour integral is $2\pi i\cdot(-i/2) = \pi$. On $C_R$, $|1/(1 + z^2)| \leq 1/(R^2 -
1)$ and the length is $\pi R$, so the arc contributes at most $\pi R/(R^2 - 1) \to 0$. Hence $\int_{-\infty}^\infty
dx/(1 + x^2) = \pi$ (@prp-residue-integrals), which $\arctan$ confirms.
:::

The third example handles an oscillating integrand with the same contour. The choice of $e^{iz}$ rather than
$\cos z$ is what makes the arc negligible.

::: {#exm-residue-theorem-fourier}
#### $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \cos x/(1 + x^2)\,dx = \pi/e$

Take $f(z) = e^{iz}/(1 + z^2)$, not $\cos z/(1 + z^2)$: on the upper arc $|e^{iz}| = e^{-\operatorname{Im} z}
\leq 1$, so the arc is negligible as before, whereas $\cos z$ grows like $e^{|\operatorname{Im} z|}$. The residue
at $i$ is $e^{-1}/(2i)$, the contour integral is $\pi/e$, and taking the real part gives the result; the imaginary
part, $\int \sin x/(1 + x^2)\,dx = 0$, is consistent with oddness (@prp-residue-integrals).
:::

The second exercise examines a contour passing between the singularities. Which residues count is a question
about the interior of the contour, not about the function.

::: {#exr-residue-theorem-outside}
#### Which poles count

Evaluate $\oint_\gamma \dfrac{dz}{(z - 1)(z - 2)}$ for $\gamma$ the circle $|z - 2| = 1/2$, the circle $|z| =
1/2$ and the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $0.5 \pm i$, $2.5 \pm i$, all positively oriented.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|z - 2| = 1/2$ encloses only $2$: $2\pi i\cdot 1 = 2\pi i$. $|z| = 1/2$ encloses neither pole: $0$ by Cauchy's
theorem. The rectangle encloses both: $2\pi i(-1 + 1) = 0$. The same function and three different answers, each
determined by the residues inside.
:::

The third exercise proves the residue-sum rule used in @exm-residue-infinity. A large circle sees all finite
residues at once and also the behaviour at infinity.

::: {#exr-residue-infinity}
#### The sum of all residues

Show that for a rational function $f$ the sum of the residues at all finite poles plus the residue at infinity is
zero, and use it to find the sum of the residues of $1/(1 + z^4)$ at its four poles without computing them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $\rho$ larger than every pole, $\oint_{|z| = \rho} f\,dz = 2\pi i\sum_{\text{finite}}\operatorname{Res}$ by the
residue theorem and $= -2\pi i\operatorname{Res}_\infty f$ by definition; adding gives the claim. $1/(1 + z^4) =
z^{-4} + \dots$ has no $1/z$ term at infinity, so the four finite residues sum to $0$, consistent with the
conjugate pairs of @exr-residue-quotient.
:::

### Worked computations

The section closes with three real integrals computed by residues, the Laurent expansions of the figure and the
series of $1/\sin z$. Each integral is given both as a real integral and as $2\pi i$ times the enclosed residues.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-residue-integrals}
#### Three real integrals by residues

$\int_{-\infty}^\infty \dfrac{dx}{1 + x^2} = \pi = 2\pi i\operatorname{Res}_{z = i}\dfrac1{1 + z^2}$,
$\int_{-\infty}^\infty \dfrac{dx}{1 + x^4} = \dfrac\pi{\sqrt2} = 2\pi i\bigl(\operatorname{Res}_{e^{i\pi/4}} +
\operatorname{Res}_{e^{3i\pi/4}}\bigr)\dfrac1{1 + z^4}$, and $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \dfrac{\cos x}{1 + x^2}\,dx =
\dfrac\pi e = 2\pi i\operatorname{Res}_{z = i}\dfrac{e^{iz}}{1 + z^2}$. Moreover $\dfrac1{(z - 1)(z - 2)} = \dfrac1{z -
2} - \dfrac1{z - 1}$ with residues $-1$ at $1$ and $1$ at $2$, its annulus partial sums at $z = 1.5i$ converge
geometrically, and $\dfrac1{\sin z} = \dfrac1z + \dfrac z6 + \dfrac{7z^3}{360} + \dots$ with residue $1$.
:::

The first example explains the general method for rational integrands over the real line. Counting degrees of numerator and denominator decides whether the arc can be discarded.

::: {#exm-residue-method-rational}
#### The method for $\int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x)/q(x)\,dx$

If $q$ has no real zeros and $\deg q \geq \deg p + 2$, then $|p/q| \leq C/R^2$ on the arc $C_R$ and the arc
contributes $O(1/R) \to 0$; the integral is $2\pi i$ times the sum of the residues in the upper half-plane. Closing
in the lower half-plane instead gives $-2\pi i$ times the lower residues, the same number.
:::

The second example explains why $e^{iz}$ replaces $\cos z$ for Fourier-type integrals. The sign of the frequency
decides the half-plane in which to close.

::: {#exm-residue-method-fourier}
#### The method for $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{ikx} r(x)\,dx$

For $k > 0$ close in the upper half-plane, where $|e^{ikz}| = e^{-k\operatorname{Im} z} \leq 1$; for $k < 0$ close
in the lower half-plane. The arc is negligible already when $\deg q \geq \deg p + 1$ (Jordan's lemma), and the
answer is $\pm 2\pi i$ times the enclosed residues. The Fourier transform of $1/(1 + x^2)$ is $\pi e^{-|k|}$.
:::

::: {#exm-residue-method-trig}
#### The method for $\int_0^{2\pi} R(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\,d\theta$

With $z = e^{i\theta}$, $\cos\theta = \tfrac12(z + 1/z)$, $\sin\theta = \tfrac1{2i}(z - 1/z)$ and $d\theta =
dz/(iz)$, the integral becomes $\oint_{|z| = 1}$ of a rational function: $\int_0^{2\pi}\dfrac{d\theta}{2 +
\cos\theta} = \oint\dfrac{2\,dz}{i(z^2 + 4z + 1)}$, with the single enclosed pole at $z = -2 + \sqrt3$, giving
$2\pi/\sqrt3$ (@exr-real-integral-trig).

The third exercise treats a pole on the contour, which requires an indentation. The half-residue rule it produces
is the one behind principal-value integrals and the $i\epsilon$ prescription.

::: {#exr-real-integral-jordan}
#### $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \sin x/x\,dx = \pi$

Integrate $e^{iz}/z$ over the contour consisting of $[-R, -\epsilon]$, the small clockwise semicircle of radius
$\epsilon$ above $0$, $[\epsilon, R]$ and the large arc $C_R$. Show that the large arc contributes nothing as
$R \to \infty$ (accept Jordan's lemma), that the small arc contributes $-i\pi$ as $\epsilon \to 0$, and conclude.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The contour encloses no singularity, so the total is $0$. On the small arc $z = \epsilon e^{i\theta}$, $\theta$
from $\pi$ to $0$: $\int e^{iz}\,dz/z = \int_\pi^0 e^{i\epsilon e^{i\theta}}\,i\,d\theta \to -i\pi$. Hence
$\lim\int_{|x| > \epsilon} e^{ix}\,dx/x = i\pi$; the real part is a principal value of an odd function, zero, and
the imaginary part gives $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \sin x/x\,dx = \pi$. A simple pole on the contour contributes
half a residue, with the sign fixed by the direction of the indentation.
:::

## Analytic continuation and special functions {#sec-analytic-continuation}

Analytic continuation, the Gamma and Beta functions, the zeta function in outline, Wick rotation as a contour
deformation. A holomorphic function is determined by its values on any small set with a limit point, so a
formula valid on a half-plane defines a function far beyond it; the Gamma and zeta functions are the standard
examples, and the rotation of an integration contour from the real to the imaginary axis, Wick rotation, is the
same principle applied to integrals.

![The Gamma function and Wick rotation. Left: $\Gamma(x)$ on the real line, with its poles at $0, -1, -2, \dots$
and the values $\Gamma(n + 1) = n!$. Right: the poles $\pm(E - i\epsilon)$ of $1/(k^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon)$ and the
counter-clockwise rotation of the real $k^0$ axis onto the imaginary axis $k^0 = ik^4$ through the two quadrants
that contain no pole. Generated by `figures/gamma_function.sage`.](figures/gamma_function.svg){#fig-gamma-function width=95%}

{{< interactive gamma_function 480 >}}

### Analytic continuation

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-analytic-continuation}
#### Analytic continuation

Let $f$ be holomorphic on a domain $D_1$ and $D_2 \supset D_1$ a larger domain. An **analytic continuation** of
$f$ to $D_2$ is a holomorphic function on $D_2$ that agrees with $f$ on $D_1$. By the **identity theorem**, two
functions holomorphic on a domain that agree on a set with a limit point in the domain (a segment, a small disc,
a convergent sequence) agree everywhere on it; hence an analytic continuation, if it exists, is unique. The
continuation may fail to exist (a natural boundary) or may depend on the path along which it is carried out, in
which case the continued function is many-valued and has branch points (@def-branch).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the geometric series, whose sum formula makes sense far beyond the disc of convergence. The
continuation is the rational function, not the series.

::: {#exm-continuation-geometric}
#### The geometric series

$\sum_{n \geq 0} z^n$ converges only on $|z| < 1$, where it equals $1/(1 - z)$; the latter is holomorphic on
$\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\}$ and is the unique analytic continuation of the series. The value $-1$ at $z = 2$ belongs
to the continuation, not to the divergent series $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots$; the zeta function below is defined by the
same mechanism.
:::

The second example shows how real identities propagate to the complex plane. Any identity between entire
functions that holds on the real axis holds everywhere.

::: {#exm-continuation-identities}
#### Identities continue

$\cos^2 z + \sin^2 z - 1$ is entire and vanishes on the real axis, a set with limit points, so it vanishes
identically: the identity holds for all complex $z$ (compare the direct proof in @exr-exp-trig). The same
argument transfers every trigonometric identity, and the functional equation $e^{z + w} = e^z e^w$, from
$\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{C}$.
:::

The third example is the logarithm, continued around the origin. The continuation exists along every path but
depends on the path, which is the origin of the branches of @sec-complex-numbers.

::: {#exm-continuation-log}
#### The logarithm continued along a loop

Start with $\operatorname{Log}$ near $z = 1$ and continue it along the unit circle counter-clockwise, disc by
disc: after a full turn the continued function is $\operatorname{Log} z + 2\pi i$. The continuation exists along
every path avoiding $0$, but its value depends on the winding of the path, so the global object is the
many-valued $\log$ with the branch point $0$.

The second exercise applies the identity theorem to functions defined by different formulas. The conclusion is
that the complex sine is the only reasonable extension of the real one.

::: {#exr-continuation-identity}
#### Uniqueness of the extension

Show that if $f$ is entire and $f(x) = \sin x$ for all real $x$ then $f = \sin$ on $\mathbb{C}$, and that no
entire function restricts to $|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f - \sin$ is entire and vanishes on $\mathbb{R}$, hence everywhere. An entire $g$ with $g(x) = |x|$ would agree
with $z$ on $(0, \infty)$ and with $-z$ on $(-\infty, 0)$, so $g = z$ and $g = -z$ on $\mathbb{C}$ by the
identity theorem, which is impossible. Non-differentiability at a single real point already forbids an entire
extension.
:::

The third exercise shows that continuation along paths can produce a many-valued function. Circling the branch
point of the square root changes the sign of the continued function.

::: {#exr-continuation-monodromy}
#### Continuation of $\sqrt z$ along a loop

Continue the principal $\sqrt z$ from $z = 1$ along the unit circle counter-clockwise by writing $z =
e^{i\theta}$ and keeping $\sqrt z = e^{i\theta/2}$ continuous, and determine the continued value at $z = 1$
after one and after two turns.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
After one turn $\theta = 2\pi$ and $\sqrt z = e^{i\pi} = -1$, the other branch; after two turns $\theta = 4\pi$
and $\sqrt z = 1$ again. The continuation is well defined along each path but depends on the path's winding
number modulo $2$: the two branches of @exm-branch-sqrt are the two values of one continued function.
:::

### The Gamma function

The factorial is defined on the non-negative integers. The Gamma function interpolates it by an integral that
converges on a half-plane, and analytic continuation then extends it to the whole plane minus a sequence of poles.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gamma-function}
#### Gamma function

The **Gamma function** is $\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ for $\operatorname{Re} z > 0$, where the
integral converges and defines a holomorphic function. Integration by parts gives the **recursion** $\Gamma(z + 1)
= z\Gamma(z)$, so $\Gamma(n + 1) = n!$ for integers $n \geq 0$. Rewriting the recursion as $\Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z +
1)/z$ continues $\Gamma$ to $\operatorname{Re} z > -1$, then to $\operatorname{Re} z > -2$, and so on: $\Gamma$ is
meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$ with simple poles at $z = 0, -1, -2, \dots$ of residue $(-1)^n/n!$ at $-n$, and no
zeros. It satisfies the **reflection formula** $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1 - z) = \pi/\sin\pi z$, whence $\Gamma(\tfrac12)
= \sqrt\pi$.
:::

The second example computes the residues at the poles from the recursion. Each step of the continuation divides
by $z + n$, and a simple pole appears.

::: {#exm-gamma-poles}
#### The poles

Near $z = 0$, $\Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z + 1)/z = (1 + O(z))/z$, a simple pole of residue $1$. Near $z = -1$,
$\Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z + 2)/\bigl(z(z + 1)\bigr) \approx 1/\bigl((-1)(z + 1)\bigr)$, residue $-1$; in general
$\operatorname{Res}_{-n}\Gamma = (-1)^n/n!$, as $\Gamma(z + n + 1)/\bigl(z(z + 1)\cdots(z + n)\bigr)$ shows.
:::

The third example is a Gaussian integral with a power of $t$, the type that appears in every loop computation.
The substitution reduces it to a Gamma function.

::: {#exm-gamma-gaussian-moments}
#### Gaussian moments

$\int_0^\infty t^{2k}e^{-t^2}\,dt = \tfrac12\Gamma(k + \tfrac12)$ with $u = t^2$, and $\int_0^\infty t^{a - 1}
e^{-\lambda t}\,dt = \Gamma(a)/\lambda^a$ for $\lambda > 0$; by analytic continuation in $\lambda$ the latter
holds for complex $\lambda$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda > 0$, with the principal power $\lambda^a$.
:::

The second exercise examines the convergence of the defining integral of the Gamma function. Both endpoints of the integral need attention, for different reasons.

::: {#exr-gamma-convergence}
#### Convergence of the integral

Show that $\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ converges absolutely exactly when $\operatorname{Re} z > 0$, and derive
the recursion $\Gamma(z + 1) = z\Gamma(z)$ by integration by parts.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|t^{z-1}| = t^{\operatorname{Re} z - 1}$. Near $0$ the integrand behaves like $t^{\operatorname{Re} z - 1}$, integrable
exactly when $\operatorname{Re} z > 0$ (@sec-riemann-integral); near $\infty$ the factor $e^{-t}$ beats any power.
Integrating by parts, $\Gamma(z + 1) = \bigl[-t^z e^{-t}\bigr]_0^\infty + z\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt =
z\Gamma(z)$, the boundary terms vanishing for $\operatorname{Re} z > 0$.
:::

The third exercise checks the reflection formula numerically at several points. It then uses the formula to
show that $\Gamma$ has no zeros.

::: {#exr-gamma-reflection}
#### The reflection formula

Check $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1 - z) = \pi/\sin\pi z$ numerically at $z = 0.3$, $z = 0.5 + 2i$ and $z = -1.7$, and
deduce from it that $\Gamma$ has no zeros.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\Gamma(z_0) = 0$ then $\pi/\sin\pi z_0 = \Gamma(z_0)\Gamma(1 - z_0)$ would vanish unless $\Gamma(1 - z_0)$
has a pole, that is, $1 - z_0 \in \{0, -1, \dots\}$, so $z_0 \in \{1, 2, \dots\}$, where $\Gamma(z_0) = (z_0 - 1)!
\neq 0$. Hence $1/\Gamma$ is entire:

{{< sage exr-gamma-reflection >}}
:::

### The Beta function

Integrals of a power of $t$ times a power of $1 - t$ appear whenever two propagators are combined. They are
expressed by a second special function, which is a ratio of Gamma functions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-beta-function}
#### Beta function

The **Beta function** is $B(a, b) = \int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1 - t)^{b-1}\,dt$ for $\operatorname{Re} a, \operatorname{Re} b >
0$. It is symmetric, $B(a, b) = B(b, a)$, and equals
$$B(a, b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a + b)},$$
which continues it meromorphically to all $(a, b)$. Equivalent forms are $B(a, b) = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}
\sin^{2a-1}\theta\cos^{2b-1}\theta\,d\theta$ and $B(a, b) = \int_0^\infty x^{a-1}(1 + x)^{-a-b}\,dx$.
:::

$B(2, 3) = \int_0^1 t(1 - t)^2\,dt = \tfrac12 - \tfrac23 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac1{12}$, and $\Gamma(2)\Gamma(3)/\Gamma(5)

The second example evaluates the Beta function at half-integers, where the trigonometric form gives the area of
a disc. The reflection formula is hidden in $B(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$.

::: {#exm-beta-half}
#### $B(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) = \pi$

$B(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) = \int_0^1 \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t(1 - t)}} = 2\int_0^{\pi/2} d\theta = \pi$ (with $t =
\sin^2\theta$), and $\Gamma(\tfrac12)^2/\Gamma(1) = \pi$ confirms $\Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt\pi$. The Wallis
integrals $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n\theta\,d\theta = \tfrac12 B(\tfrac{n+1}2, \tfrac12)$ are the same function.
:::

The third example is the volume of the unit ball, which combines the Gamma and Beta functions. The formula is
used in dimensional regularisation, where $n$ is continued to non-integer values.

::: {#exm-beta-ball-volume}
#### The volume of the unit ball in $n$ dimensions

Integrating the Gaussian $e^{-|x|^2}$ over $\mathbb{R}^n$ in Cartesian and in polar coordinates, $\pi^{n/2} =
S_{n-1}\int_0^\infty r^{n-1}e^{-r^2}\,dr = S_{n-1}\tfrac12\Gamma(\tfrac n2)$, so the area of the unit sphere is
$S_{n-1} = 2\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(\tfrac n2)$ and the volume of the unit ball is $V_n = S_{n-1}/n =
\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(\tfrac n2 + 1)$: $V_2 = \pi$, $V_3 = \tfrac43\pi$, and $V_n$ makes sense for any complex $n$.
:::

The second exercise derives the trigonometric and the rational forms of the Beta function by substitution.
These are the forms that appear in angular integrals and in @exr-ca-keyhole-beta.

::: {#exr-beta-trig}
#### Three forms of the Beta function

Derive $B(a, b) = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2a-1}\theta\cos^{2b-1}\theta\,d\theta$ and $B(a, b) = \int_0^\infty
x^{a-1}(1 + x)^{-a-b}\,dx$ from the definition by substitution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $t = \sin^2\theta$, $dt = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$ and $1 - t = \cos^2\theta$, giving the first form.
With $t = x/(1 + x)$, $1 - t = 1/(1 + x)$ and $dt = dx/(1 + x)^2$, so $t^{a-1}(1 - t)^{b-1}dt = x^{a-1}(1 +
x)^{-(a-1) - (b-1) - 2}dx = x^{a-1}(1 + x)^{-a-b}dx$.
:::

The third exercise proves the relation between Beta and Gamma. The product of two Gamma integrals is a double
integral, and polar coordinates separate it.

::: {#exr-beta-gamma-derivation}
#### $B = \Gamma\Gamma/\Gamma$

Prove $B(a, b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a + b)$ by writing $\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)$ as a double integral over
the quadrant and changing to the variables $s = u + v$, $t = u/(u + v)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) = \int_0^\infty\!\!\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}v^{b-1}e^{-u-v}\,du\,dv$. With $u = st$, $v = s(1 -
t)$, the Jacobian (@sec-calculus) is $s$, and the integrand becomes $s^{a+b-1}t^{a-1}(1 - t)^{b-1}e^{-s}$; the
$s$-integral over $(0, \infty)$ gives $\Gamma(a + b)$ and the $t$-integral over $(0, 1)$ gives $B(a, b)$.
:::

### The zeta function

The Riemann zeta function is the archetype of a function defined by a series on a half-plane and continued
beyond it. Its values at negative integers, finite numbers assigned to divergent sums, are what zeta-function
regularisation uses.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-zeta-function}
#### Zeta function

The **Riemann zeta function** is $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n \geq 1} n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, where the
series converges absolutely (@sec-series) and defines a holomorphic function. It has the **Euler product**
$\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$ over the primes, and it continues analytically to a meromorphic function on
$\mathbb{C}$ with a single simple pole at $s = 1$ of residue $1$, satisfying the functional equation
$\zeta(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin(\tfrac{\pi s}2)\Gamma(1 - s)\zeta(1 - s)$. The continuation is outlined in
@exm-zeta-continuation; its values include $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$, $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$, $\zeta(-1) = -
\tfrac1{12}$ and $\zeta(-2n) = 0$ for $n \geq 1$.
:::

#### $\zeta(2)$ and $\zeta(4)$

$\zeta(2) = 1 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac19 + \dots = \pi^2/6$ (the Basel problem) and $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$
(@prp-gamma-values); in general $\zeta(2n) = (-1)^{n+1}B_{2n}(2\pi)^{2n}/(2(2n)!)$ with the Bernoulli numbers
$B_2 = \tfrac16$, $B_4 = -\tfrac1{30}$. The residue theorem applied to $\pi\cot(\pi z)/z^{2n}$ is one proof.
:::

The second example sketches the analytic continuation by one step. A convergent alternating series extends
$\zeta$ to the critical strip, and the functional equation carries it to the rest of the plane.

::: {#exm-zeta-continuation}
#### Continuation past the pole

For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, $\bigl(1 - 2^{1-s}\bigr)\zeta(s) = \sum_{n \geq 1}(-1)^{n+1}n^{-s}$ (subtract twice
the even terms). The right side converges for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, so $\zeta(s) = (1 - 2^{1-s})^{-1}
\sum(-1)^{n+1}n^{-s}$ continues $\zeta$ to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ with the pole at $s = 1$ coming from the
prefactor; the functional equation then gives $\operatorname{Re} s \leq 0$. At $s = 0$ the alternating series
$1 - 1 + 1 - \dots$ is interpreted as $\tfrac12$ and $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$.
:::

The third example is the value $\zeta(-1) = -1/12$, often written as the sum of all positive integers. The
example says precisely in what sense that statement is true.

::: {#exm-zeta-minus-one}
#### "$1 + 2 + 3 + \dots = -\tfrac1{12}$"

The series $\sum n$ diverges; $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac1{12}$ is the value at $s = -1$ of the analytic continuation of
$\sum n^{-s}$. Concretely, $\sum_{n \geq 1} n e^{-\epsilon n} = \dfrac{e^{-\epsilon}}{(1 - e^{-\epsilon})^2} =
\dfrac1{\epsilon^2} - \dfrac1{12} + O(\epsilon^2)$: the regularised sum is a divergent term plus the finite part
$-\tfrac1{12}$ (@exr-zeta-regularised-sum). This is how zeta-function regularisation assigns finite values to
sums over modes.
:::

The second exercise derives the Euler product from unique factorisation. Expanding each factor as a geometric
series and multiplying out produces every integer exactly once.

::: {#exr-zeta-euler-product}
#### The Euler product

Show that for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, $\prod_{p \leq N}(1 - p^{-s})^{-1} = \sum' n^{-s}$, the sum over integers
whose prime factors are all at most $N$, and deduce the Euler product as $N \to \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(1 - p^{-s})^{-1} = \sum_{k \geq 0} p^{-ks}$; multiplying finitely many absolutely convergent series, the product
is $\sum p_1^{-k_1 s}\cdots p_r^{-k_r s}$ over all exponent tuples, that is, $\sum n^{-s}$ over the $n$ whose
factorisation uses only $p_1, \dots, p_r$, each $n$ once by unique factorisation. As $N \to \infty$ every $n$ is
included and the tail $\sum_{n > N}|n^{-s}|$ tends to $0$.
:::

#### A regularised sum

\dots$ with finite part $-\tfrac1{12} = \zeta(-1)$:

### Wick rotation

An integral over the real line of a function holomorphic in a sector can be moved to another ray through the
origin. Rotating the real axis to the imaginary axis is called Wick rotation, and it converts oscillatory
integrals into decaying ones.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-wick-rotation}
#### Wick rotation

Let $f$ be holomorphic on an open set containing the closed first and third quadrants of the $k^0$-plane, except
possibly at infinity, with $|k^0 f(k^0)| \to 0$ uniformly as $|k^0| \to \infty$ in those quadrants. The **Wick
rotation** is the identity
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(k^0)\,dk^0 = i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(ik^4)\,dk^4,$$
obtained from Cauchy's theorem on the closed contour made of the real axis, the imaginary axis traversed
downward and two arcs at infinity in the first and third quadrants: the arcs vanish by the ML estimate and the
contour encloses no singularity. The substitution $k^0 = ik^4$ (or $t = -i\tau$ in position space) is the
**rotation to Euclidean signature**: a Minkowski square $(k^0)^2 - \mathbf{k}^2$ becomes $-\bigl((k^4)^2 +
\mathbf{k}^2\bigr)$, minus a Euclidean square.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the rotation that makes propagators Euclidean. The $i\epsilon$ displaces the poles out of the
rotated quadrants, which is the reason for the prescription.

::: {#exm-wick-propagator}
#### The $i\epsilon$ prescription

$f(k^0) = 1/\bigl((k^0)^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon\bigr)$ has poles at $k^0 = \pm(E - i\epsilon/2E)$, one in the fourth
and one in the second quadrant (@fig-gamma-function), so the first and third quadrants are pole-free and the
rotation is allowed: $\int dk^0/\bigl((k^0)^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon\bigr) = i\int dk^4/\bigl(-(k^4)^2 - E^2\bigr) = -
i\pi/E$ (@prp-wick-rotation). With the opposite sign, $-i\epsilon$, the poles would sit in the rotated quadrants
and the rotation would have to be clockwise.
:::

The second example rotates a Gaussian, turning a Fresnel integral into a real one. The arcs vanish only in a
sector, which is why the rotation angle is $\pi/4$ here rather than $\pi/2$.

::: {#exm-wick-fresnel}
#### The Fresnel integral

$\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{iat^2}\,dt$ ($a > 0$) is oscillatory. Rotating $t = e^{i\pi/4}u$, the exponent becomes
$ia\,e^{i\pi/2}u^2 = -au^2$ and the arcs in the sector $0 \leq \arg t \leq \pi/4$ vanish ($\operatorname{Re}(it^2)
= -a|t|^2\sin 2\arg t \leq 0$ there), so $\int e^{iat^2}\,dt = e^{i\pi/4}\sqrt{\pi/a}$ (@exr-wick-gaussian). The
real-time path integral of a free particle is of this type.
:::

The third example is the rotation in position space. The oscillating weight $e^{iS}$ of a real-time path integral
becomes the decaying weight $e^{-S_E}$ of a statistical sum.

::: {#exm-wick-action}
#### From $e^{iS}$ to $e^{-S_E}$

For $S = \int dt\bigl(\tfrac12 m\dot x^2 - V(x)\bigr)$, the substitution $t = -i\tau$ gives $dt = -i\,d\tau$ and
$\dot x = i\,dx/d\tau$, so $iS = -\int d\tau\bigl(\tfrac12 m (dx/d\tau)^2 + V(x)\bigr) = -S_E$, the negative of the
Euclidean action, in which the potential has changed sign relative to the kinetic term
(@exr-wick-euclidean-action). Oscillatory weights become damped ones, and quantum mechanics in imaginary time looks
like statistical mechanics.
:::

::: {#exr-wick-gaussian}
#### The Fresnel integral by rotation

Compute $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{it^2}\,dt$ with Sage, compare with $e^{i\pi/4}\sqrt\pi$, and derive the latter
from the rotation of @exm-wick-fresnel and the Gaussian integral $\int e^{-u^2}\,du = \sqrt\pi$.

$e^{i\pi/4}\sqrt\pi = \sqrt{\pi/2}(1 + i)$; real and imaginary parts are the two Fresnel integrals $\int\cos t^2 =
\int\sin t^2 = \sqrt{\pi/2}$:

{{< sage exr-wick-gaussian >}}

The second exercise verifies the vanishing of the arcs for the propagator. The ML estimate of @def-contour-integral

::: {#exr-wick-arcs}
#### The arcs at infinity

Show that the integral of $1/\bigl((k^0)^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon\bigr)$ over the arc $k^0 = Re^{i\theta}$, $0 \leq
\theta \leq \pi/2$, tends to $0$ as $R \to \infty$, and that the same holds for $e^{-ik^0 t}/\bigl((k^0)^2 - E^2 +
i\epsilon\bigr)$ only when $t$ has the right sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the arc $|(k^0)^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon| \geq R^2 - E^2 - \epsilon$ and the length is $\pi R/2$, so the integral is
at most $\pi R/\bigl(2(R^2 - E^2 - \epsilon)\bigr) \to 0$. With the factor $e^{-ik^0 t}$, $|e^{-ik^0 t}| =
e^{t\operatorname{Im} k^0} = e^{tR\sin\theta}$, bounded on the upper arc only for $t \leq 0$; for $t > 0$ one must
close in the lower half-plane instead, which is the computation of @exr-ca-propagator-time.
:::

The third exercise carries out the rotation of the action in detail. Keeping track of the factors of $i$ is the
whole exercise.

::: {#exr-wick-euclidean-action}
#### The Euclidean action

Substitute $t = -i\tau$ in $S = \int dt\bigl(\tfrac12 m\dot x^2 - V\bigr)$ and in the quadratic Lagrangian
$\tfrac12(\partial_t\phi)^2 - \tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2 - \tfrac12 m^2\phi^2$ of a field, and show that $iS = -S_E$
with $S_E = \int d\tau\bigl(\tfrac12 m x'^2 + V\bigr)$ and $S_E = \int d\tau\,d^3x\,\tfrac12\bigl((\partial_\tau\phi)^2 +
(\nabla\phi)^2 + m^2\phi^2\bigr)$ respectively.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dt = -i\,d\tau$ and $\partial_t = i\partial_\tau$, so $\dot x^2 = -x'^2$ and $(\partial_t\phi)^2 = -
(\partial_\tau\phi)^2$. Then $iS = i\int(-i\,d\tau)\bigl(-\tfrac12 m x'^2 - V\bigr) = -\int d\tau\bigl(\tfrac12 m
x'^2 + V\bigr)$, and for the field $iS = \int d\tau\,d^3x\bigl(-\tfrac12(\partial_\tau\phi)^2 - \tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2 -
\tfrac12 m^2\phi^2\bigr) = -S_E$. The Euclidean action is positive, which is what makes $e^{-S_E}$ a usable
weight.
:::

### Worked computations

The section closes with two propositions of explicit values, one on the special functions and
one on the Wick rotation of the propagator integral. Both are collections of small identities that every later
use of these functions relies on.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-gamma-values}
#### Values of the special functions

$\Gamma(n + 1) = n!$ for $n = 0, \dots, 10$; $\Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt\pi$, $\Gamma(\tfrac52) = \tfrac34\sqrt\pi$,
$\Gamma(-\tfrac12) = -2\sqrt\pi$; $\operatorname{Res}_{-n}\Gamma = (-1)^n/n!$ for $n = 0, \dots, 4$; $B(2, 3) =
\tfrac1{12} = \Gamma(2)\Gamma(3)/\Gamma(5)$ and $B(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) = \pi$; $\Gamma(\tfrac14)\Gamma(\tfrac34) =
\pi\sqrt2$ (numerically, to $10^{-12}$); $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$, $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$, $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$,
$\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac1{12}$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example derives the Gamma values of the proposition from the recursion $\Gamma(z + 1) = z\Gamma(z)$ and
the reflection formula. Only $\Gamma(1) = 1$ and $\Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt\pi$ are needed as starting values.

::: {#exm-gamma-check-method}
#### Values from the recursion and the reflection formula

From $\Gamma(1) = 1$ the recursion gives $\Gamma(n + 1) = n\Gamma(n) = \dots = n!$. From $\Gamma(\tfrac12) =
\sqrt\pi$ it gives $\Gamma(\tfrac52) = \tfrac32\cdot\tfrac12\sqrt\pi = \tfrac34\sqrt\pi$ upwards and
$\Gamma(-\tfrac12) = \Gamma(\tfrac12)/(-\tfrac12) = -2\sqrt\pi$ downwards. Neither $\Gamma(\tfrac14)$ nor
$\Gamma(\tfrac34)$ is reached this way, but their product is: $\Gamma(\tfrac14)\Gamma(\tfrac34) = \pi/\sin(\pi/4) =
\pi\sqrt2$ by the reflection formula.
:::

The second example extends the half-integer values to a closed formula for all $n$. Induction on the recursion is all that the proof takes.

::: {#exm-gamma-half-integer-formula}
#### $\Gamma(n + \tfrac12)$

$\Gamma(n + \tfrac12) = (n - \tfrac12)(n - \tfrac32)\cdots\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt\pi = \dfrac{(2n)!}{4^n n!}\sqrt\pi$:
$\Gamma(\tfrac32) = \tfrac12\sqrt\pi$, $\Gamma(\tfrac52) = \tfrac34\sqrt\pi$, $\Gamma(\tfrac72) = \tfrac{15}8\sqrt\pi$
(@exr-gamma-half-integers). These are the Gamma functions of the volumes of odd-dimensional balls in
@exm-beta-ball-volume.
:::

The third example uses the values to compute the area of spheres. The formula interpolates between dimensions,
which is the starting point of dimensional regularisation.

::: {#exm-gamma-sphere-areas}
#### Areas of spheres

$S_{n-1} = 2\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(\tfrac n2)$ gives $S_1 = 2\pi$, $S_2 = 2\pi^{3/2}/\Gamma(\tfrac32) = 4\pi$, $S_3 =
2\pi^2$, and for $n = 4 - 2\varepsilon$ the expansion $S_{3 - 2\varepsilon} = 2\pi^2\bigl(1 + \varepsilon(1 -
\gamma_E - \ln\pi) + \dots\bigr)$, where the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma_E = -\Gamma'(1)$ appears, as it does
in every dimensionally regularised loop integral.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves the half-integer formula and checks it in Sage. The exact simplification of
$\Gamma(n + \tfrac12)$ is a good test of the recursion.

::: {#exr-gamma-half-integers}
#### Half-integer values

Prove $\Gamma(n + \tfrac12) = \dfrac{(2n)!}{4^n n!}\sqrt\pi$ by induction and check it with Sage for $n = 0,
\dots, 6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $n = 0$ it is $\Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt\pi$. If it holds for $n$, then $\Gamma(n + \tfrac32) = (n +
\tfrac12)\Gamma(n + \tfrac12) = \dfrac{(2n + 1)}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(2n)!}{4^n n!}\sqrt\pi = \dfrac{(2n + 2)!}{4^{n+1}(n +
1)!}\sqrt\pi$, since $(2n + 2)! = (2n + 2)(2n + 1)(2n)!$ and $(2n + 2)/(4(n + 1)) = \tfrac12$:

{{< sage exr-gamma-half-integers >}}
:::

The second exercise checks Legendre's duplication formula for the Gamma function. The check is exact at integers and half-integers, and numerical elsewhere.

::: {#exr-gamma-duplication}
#### Legendre's duplication formula

Check $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(z + \tfrac12) = 2^{1 - 2z}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(2z)$ exactly for $z = 1, 2, 3, \tfrac72$ and
numerically for $z = 0.3 + 0.7i$, and use it to express $\Gamma(\tfrac14)\Gamma(\tfrac34)$ through
$\Gamma(\tfrac12)$ and the reflection formula.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Reflection at $z = \tfrac14$ gives $\Gamma(\tfrac14)\Gamma(\tfrac34) = \pi/\sin(\pi/4) = \pi\sqrt2$ directly;
duplication at $z = \tfrac14$ gives instead $\Gamma(\tfrac14)\Gamma(\tfrac34) = 2^{1/2}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(\tfrac12) =
\sqrt2\,\pi$, the same:

{{< sage exr-gamma-duplication >}}
:::

The third exercise derives the residues of $\Gamma$ at all its poles from the recursion. It is the computation of @exm-gamma-poles made general, with the reflection formula as a bonus.

::: {#exr-gamma-residues}
#### The residues of $\Gamma$

Prove $\operatorname{Res}_{z = -n}\Gamma(z) = (-1)^n/n!$ from the recursion, and deduce from the reflection formula
that $1/\Gamma$ is entire with simple zeros exactly at $0, -1, -2, \dots$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Iterating, $\Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z + n + 1)/\bigl(z(z + 1)\cdots(z + n)\bigr)$; near $z = -n$ the numerator tends to
$\Gamma(1) = 1$ and the product of the other factors to $(-n)(-n + 1)\cdots(-1) = (-1)^n n!$, so $(z +
n)\Gamma(z) \to (-1)^n/n!$. $1/\Gamma(z) = \Gamma(1 - z)\sin(\pi z)/\pi$: the zeros of $\sin\pi z$ at the positive
integers are cancelled by the poles of $\Gamma(1 - z)$, and those at $0, -1, \dots$ remain simple zeros.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The Wick rotation of the propagator integral is the second proposition. The two sides of the rotation identity
are computed independently, one by residues and one as a real integral.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-wick-rotation}
#### Wick rotation of the propagator integral

For $E > 0$ and $\delta > 0$ let $h(k) = 1/\bigl((k - (E - i\delta))(k - (-E + i\delta))\bigr)$, the propagator
denominator with its poles displaced. Then $2\pi i\operatorname{Res}_{k = -E + i\delta} h \to -i\pi/E$ as $\delta
\to 0$, the Euclidean integral $\int_{-\infty}^\infty dk/(k^2 + E^2)$ equals $\pi/E$, and the two agree with the
rotation identity $\int dk^0\,f = i\int dk^4\,f(ik^4) = -i\pi/E$; numerically, with $E = 1$ and $\epsilon =
10^{-4}$, the imaginary part of $\int dk^0/\bigl((k^0)^2 - 1 + i\epsilon\bigr)$ is $-\pi$ to $10^{-3}$.
:::

The first example reads the residue computation as a closing of the contour in the upper half-plane. It is the
semicircular contour of @sec-residues once more.

::: {#exm-wick-by-residues}
#### The Minkowski integral by residues

$h$ decays like $1/k^2$, so the upper arc is negligible and $\int_{-\infty}^\infty h\,dk = 2\pi i\operatorname{Res}_{-E +
i\delta} h = 2\pi i/\bigl(-2E + 2i\delta\bigr) \to -i\pi/E$. Closing in the lower half-plane gives $-2\pi i\cdot
1/(2E - 2i\delta)$, the same limit, as it must.
:::

The second example performs the Euclidean side. The integral is elementary, and the factor $i$ from $dk^0 = i\,dk^4$
produces the agreement.

::: {#exm-wick-euclidean-side}
#### The Euclidean integral

$i\int_{-\infty}^\infty \dfrac{dk^4}{(ik^4)^2 - E^2} = -i\int_{-\infty}^\infty\dfrac{dk^4}{(k^4)^2 + E^2} = -
i\cdot\dfrac\pi E$: the $\epsilon$ can be dropped on the Euclidean side, since $(k^4)^2 + E^2$ never vanishes.
This is why Euclidean propagators need no $i\epsilon$.
:::

The third example explains the role of the numerical check. The symbolic computation treats $\delta$ as a
parameter, the numerical one takes a small concrete value.

::: {#exm-wick-numerical-check}
#### The numerical check

With $E = 1$ and $\epsilon = 10^{-4}$ the integrand $1/(k^2 - 1 + i\epsilon)$ is sharply peaked near $k = \pm1$;
`numerical_integral` over $[-500, 500]$ of its imaginary part gives $-\pi$ to three decimals, the real part being
a principal value that vanishes by oddness about each peak. The decomposition $\dfrac1{x + i\epsilon} \to
\mathrm{P}\dfrac1x - i\pi\delta(x)$ is being observed.
:::

**Sage.** Sage integrates 1/(k^2 - E^2 + i eps) exactly and checks |Im + pi/E| <= pi eps^2/(2E^5) and |Re| <= pi eps/(2E^3) (the larger ratio <= 1); E = 1, eps = 1e-4 is the proposition, E = 2 the exercise; Sage integrates 1/(k^2 - E^2 + i eps) over R and compares with -pi i/c for the root c of c^2 = E^2 - i eps with Im c < 0; Sage integrates i/((i k)^2 - E^2) over R and compares with -i pi/E.
:::

The second exercise examines the opposite sign of $i\epsilon$. The poles move into the other quadrants and the
rotation must be clockwise, which changes the sign of the result.

::: {#exr-wick-sign}
#### The other prescription

Repeat the residue computation for $1/(k^2 - E^2 - i\epsilon)$ and show that the integral is $+i\pi/E$; explain
why the Wick rotation for this integrand is clockwise, $k^0 = -ik^4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Now the poles are $E + i\delta$ (first quadrant) and $-E - i\delta$ (third); closing above picks up $2\pi
i/(2E) = i\pi/E$. The first and third quadrants contain poles, so the counter-clockwise rotation is forbidden; the
second and fourth are free, and rotating clockwise, $k^0 = -ik^4$, gives $-i\int dk^4/\bigl(-(k^4)^2 - E^2\bigr) =
i\pi/E$. The two prescriptions are complex conjugates of each other, as the integrands are.
:::

The third exercise rotates the Gaussian path-integral weight. It shows that Wick rotation also fixes the
convergence of real-time Gaussian integrals.

::: {#exr-wick-gaussian-action}
#### A Gaussian with an $i\epsilon$

Evaluate $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{\frac i2(a + i\epsilon)x^2}\,dx$ for $a > 0$, $\epsilon > 0$, both by completing
the rotation to $x = e^{i\pi/4}u$ and by analytic continuation of $\int e^{-\frac12\lambda x^2}\,dx =
\sqrt{2\pi/\lambda}$ in $\lambda$; identify the branch of the square root.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\lambda = -i(a + i\epsilon) = \epsilon - ia$ has positive real part, so the Gaussian formula continues to it:
$\sqrt{2\pi/(\epsilon - ia)} \to \sqrt{2\pi/a}\,e^{i\pi/4}$ as $\epsilon \to 0$, with the principal branch (the
continuation starts from $\lambda > 0$ and never crosses the cut). The rotation gives $e^{i\pi/4}\int
e^{-\frac12 a u^2}\,du = e^{i\pi/4}\sqrt{2\pi/a}$, the same value; the $i\epsilon$ makes the original integral
absolutely convergent, which the rotation then evaluates.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-complex-analysis-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three exercises of this section combine several sections of the chapter. The first evaluates a Fourier
transform by shifting a contour, the second integrates around a branch cut with a keyhole contour and produces the
reflection formula of the Gamma function, and the third derives the time-dependent propagator from the residues of
the $i\epsilon$-displaced poles. The first integrative exercise is the shifted Gaussian. Cauchy's theorem on a
rectangle moves the integration line into the complex plane, where the integral becomes the familiar real one.

::: {#exr-ca-gaussian-fourier}
#### The Fourier transform of a Gaussian

Show that $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}e^{ikx}\,dx = \sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-k^2/2}$ for real $k$ by completing the
square and shifting the contour from $\operatorname{Im} x = 0$ to $\operatorname{Im} x = k$ (Cauchy's theorem of
@sec-contour-integration on a rectangle); confirm with Sage. Why is a Gaussian its own Fourier transform?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-x^2/2 + ikx = -(x - ik)^2/2 - k^2/2$. The integrand $e^{-(x - ik)^2/2}$ is entire, and on the vertical sides of
the rectangle $[-R, R] \times [0, k]$ it is bounded by $e^{-R^2/2 + k^2/2} \to 0$, so by @thm-cauchy
$\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-(x - ik)^2/2}\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-u^2/2}\,du = \sqrt{2\pi}$ (@exm-gamma-values with
$u^2 = 2t$). The transform of $e^{-x^2/2}$ is $\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}$, the same Gaussian up to the normalisation:
the Gaussian is an eigenfunction of the Fourier transform. Sage's `integrate` agrees, and the Gaussian integral
itself is $\Gamma(\tfrac12)\sqrt2$:

{{< sage exr-ca-gaussian-fourier >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise integrates a many-valued function around its branch cut. The discontinuity across
the cut, the residue at a pole and the Beta function combine to prove the reflection formula of the Gamma function.

::: {#exr-ca-keyhole-beta}
#### A keyhole contour and the reflection formula

For $0 < a < 1$ evaluate $I(a) = \int_0^\infty \dfrac{x^{a-1}}{1 + x}\,dx$ by integrating $z^{a-1}/(1 + z)$, with
the branch $\arg z \in (0, 2\pi)$ (@def-branch), over the keyhole contour that runs along the upper side of the
positive real axis, around a large circle, back along the lower side and around a small circle about $0$.
Deduce from @def-beta-function that $\Gamma(a)\Gamma(1 - a) = \pi/\sin\pi a$, and check $I(\tfrac13) =
2\pi/\sqrt3$ with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the upper side $z^{a-1} = x^{a-1}$; on the lower side $\arg z = 2\pi$ and $z^{a-1} = x^{a-1}e^{2\pi i(a-1)} =
x^{a-1}e^{2\pi ia}$, traversed in the opposite direction. The large circle contributes $O(R^{a-1}) \to 0$ and the
small one $O(\epsilon^a) \to 0$. The only pole inside is $z = -1 = e^{i\pi}$, with residue $e^{i\pi(a-1)} = -
e^{i\pi a}$ (@def-residue). By @thm-residue, $(1 - e^{2\pi ia})I(a) = -2\pi i\,e^{i\pi a}$, so $I(a) =
\dfrac{-2\pi i}{e^{-i\pi a} - e^{i\pi a}} = \dfrac{\pi}{\sin\pi a}$. The rational form of the Beta function gives
$I(a) = B(a, 1 - a) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(1 - a)/\Gamma(1)$, which is the reflection formula; at $a = \tfrac13$ both
sides equal $2\pi/\sqrt3$ (@exr-gamma-recursion):

{{< sage exr-ca-keyhole-beta >}}
:::

The third integrative exercise evaluates the time-dependent propagator from the $i\epsilon$-displaced poles. Which
pole contributes depends on the sign of the time, and the answer explains the Feynman prescription.

::: {#exr-ca-propagator-time}
#### The propagator in time

Evaluate $G(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \dfrac{dk^0}{2\pi}\,\dfrac{e^{-ik^0 t}}{(k^0)^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon}$ for $t >
0$ and for $t < 0$ by closing the contour in the half-plane where $e^{-ik^0 t}$ decays (@exr-wick-arcs), and show
that $G(t) = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-iE|t|}$ as $\epsilon \to 0$. Which pole contributes for each sign of $t$, and what
does the answer say about the frequencies that propagate forward and backward in time?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The poles are $k^0 = E - i\delta$ and $k^0 = -E + i\delta$ with $\delta = \epsilon/2E$ (@exm-wick-propagator). For
$t > 0$, $|e^{-ik^0 t}| = e^{t\operatorname{Im} k^0}$ decays in the lower half-plane, so close below (clockwise):
$G = \dfrac1{2\pi}\cdot(-2\pi i)\operatorname{Res}_{E - i\delta} = -i\,\dfrac{e^{-iEt}}{2E}$ in the limit. For $t <
0$ close above and pick up $-E + i\delta$: $G = \dfrac1{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi i\cdot\dfrac{e^{iEt}}{-2E} = -i\,\dfrac{e^{-iE|t|}}{2E}$.
Hence $G(t) = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-iE|t|}$: the positive-frequency pole $k^0 = +E$ propagates forward in time and the
negative-frequency pole $k^0 = -E$ backward, which is the content of the Feynman prescription and the reason
the $i\epsilon$ is placed as it is. The Wick-rotated version, $t = -i\tau$, is $G = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-E|\tau|}$, a
decaying Euclidean propagator, consistent with @prp-wick-rotation at $\tau = 0$ after the factor $i$ from $dk^0 =
i\,dk^4$ is included.
:::
